title: Don't block on async code
description: Prefer `async`/`await` all the way down; avoid blocking on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()` — it risks thread-pool starvation and deadlocks, especially under a `SynchronizationContext`.
why: Blocking a thread that's actually waiting on I/O wastes a pool thread and can deadlock when the awaited continuation needs the same captured context to resume.
scenario: A logistics company's ASP.NET MVC API called `.Result` on an async repository call inside a controller action; under peak shipping-season load the captured SynchronizationContext deadlocked and the whole app pool froze until it was recycled.

title: Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
description: Library code with no UI/request context to resume on should use `ConfigureAwait(false)` so continuations don't unnecessarily marshal back to a captured context.
why: Marshaling back to a captured context costs a thread hop on every await, and library code has no reason to resume on a UI/request context it doesn't own.
scenario: A shared internal NuGet package used across a bank's microservices omitted ConfigureAwait(false) in its HTTP client wrapper; consumed from a WinForms internal tool, every call needlessly marshaled back to the UI thread and made batch imports visibly sluggish.

title: Avoid async void outside event handlers
description: `async void` methods can't be awaited and their exceptions can't be caught by the caller — reserve the pattern for event handlers and use `async Task` everywhere else.
why: An unhandled exception from `async void` crashes the process instead of surfacing to a caller who could catch it, making the failure far harder to diagnose.
scenario: A payments team wired an `async void` handler to a message-bus event; an unhandled exception inside it crashed the whole worker process instead of failing just that one message, taking down consumption for the entire queue.

title: Return Task, not void, for anything awaitable
description: Any method you need to await, test, or compose with other async work should return `Task`/`Task<T>` so callers can observe completion and exceptions.
why: Only a `Task` gives the caller a way to await completion, observe exceptions, and compose the work with other async operations.
scenario: A healthcare scheduling API had a notification-sending method written as `async void` for convenience; QA couldn't write a test that awaited it, and a silent failure to send appointment reminders went unnoticed for weeks.

title: Reuse HttpClient instances
description: Create a single `HttpClient` (or resolve one via `IHttpClientFactory`) instead of `new HttpClient()` per call — repeated instantiation can exhaust available sockets under load.
why: Each new `HttpClient` opens its own socket pool, and under load the OS can run out of available ports before old sockets are released.
scenario: An e-commerce integrations team instantiated a fresh HttpClient per outbound call to a shipping-rate API; under Black Friday load the app exhausted ephemeral ports and started throwing SocketException until they switched to IHttpClientFactory.

title: Dispose deterministically with using
description: Wrap `IDisposable` resources in `using`/`await using` instead of relying on the finalizer, which runs at an unpredictable time and adds GC pressure.
why: The finalizer runs on its own unpredictable schedule, so unmanaged handles and memory can pile up long after you're actually done with them.
scenario: A file-processing service at a media company left FileStream objects to be cleaned up by the finalizer instead of a using block; under sustained load it ran out of file handles and started failing uploads until the leak was traced to the missing disposal.

title: Avoid unnecessary boxing
description: Don't box value types into non-generic collections (`ArrayList`) or through interface calls in hot paths — each box is a heap allocation and a copy.
why: Each box is a heap allocation the GC has to track and later collect — doing it in a hot loop turns cheap value-type work into allocation pressure.
scenario: An analytics team's hot aggregation loop stored millions of int values in an ArrayList; profiling a slow nightly report showed most of the time went to boxing allocations and GC pressure, not the actual math.

title: Use StringBuilder for loop concatenation
description: Repeated `+=` string concatenation in a loop allocates a new string each iteration; use `StringBuilder` when building a string incrementally.
why: Strings are immutable, so `+=` in a loop allocates and copies a new string every iteration — O(n²) work for what should be O(n).
scenario: A reporting service built a multi-megabyte CSV export using += inside a loop over hundreds of thousands of rows; an export that should take seconds took minutes until it was rewritten with StringBuilder.

title: Prefer records for immutable data
description: Use `record` types for data-carrying types that need value equality and immutability instead of hand-rolling `Equals`/`GetHashCode` on a class.
why: Hand-rolled `Equals`/`GetHashCode` is easy to get subtly wrong — a forgotten field or an inconsistent hash — and records give you correct value semantics for free.
scenario: A trading firm's market-data DTOs used hand-rolled Equals/GetHashCode that forgot a newly added field, causing duplicate detection to silently miss records; switching to record types fixed the value-equality bug for free.

title: Turn on nullable reference types and fix the warnings
description: Enable `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` project-wide and actually resolve the warnings it surfaces instead of suppressing them — that's where the real value is.
why: Most production `NullReferenceException`s are preventable at compile time — suppressing the warnings just defers the same bug to runtime.
scenario: An insurance company enabled nullable reference types on a legacy claims service and surfaced over a hundred real, previously invisible null-dereference risks the team had been debugging one production NullReferenceException at a time.

title: Use Span<T> for high-throughput buffer work
description: Reach for `Span<T>`/`Memory<T>` in parsing or buffer-manipulation hot paths to avoid allocating intermediate substrings or arrays.
why: Substrings and array slices allocate a new copy every time; `Span<T>` lets you operate on a view of existing memory instead.
scenario: A telecom's protocol parser allocated a new byte-array substring for every frame it decoded; switching the hot parsing path to Span<T> cut allocations sharply and reduced GC pauses on a service processing millions of frames a day.

title: Favor DI over static singletons
description: Inject dependencies rather than reaching for static singletons or service locators — it keeps code testable and dependencies explicit.
why: A static/singleton dependency is invisible in a class's constructor, so tests can't substitute it and the class's real requirements stay hidden.
scenario: A legacy inventory system relied on a static `CacheManager.Instance` accessed from dozens of classes; when the team tried to unit test order processing, they couldn't substitute a fake cache and needed a real Redis connection just to run a test.

title: Keep constructors free of virtual calls
description: Calling a virtual method from a constructor can run against a derived object that isn't fully initialized yet — keep constructors non-virtual and simple.
why: A virtual call made during construction can execute against a derived class whose own fields aren't initialized yet, producing bugs that only surface in subclasses.
scenario: A base `Shape` class called an overridable `Initialize()` from its constructor; a derived `Circle` subclass's own field initializers hadn't run yet when Initialize executed, producing a null-radius bug that only showed up in the subclass.

title: Implement IEquatable<T> for hot equality checks
description: Types used as dictionary/hash-set keys or compared frequently should implement `IEquatable<T>` (or be records) to avoid the boxing/reflection cost of default `Equals`.
why: The default equality check for a struct can box and use reflection, which is measurably slower than a hand-written or record-generated comparison in a hot path.
scenario: A geospatial service used millions of coordinate structs as dictionary keys; default equality's boxing and reflection made lookups a measurable hot spot until the struct implemented IEquatable<T> directly.

title: Expose read-only collection types in public APIs
description: Return `IReadOnlyList<T>`/`IReadOnlyCollection<T>` from public APIs that don't need to expose mutation, rather than a concrete `List<T>`.
why: Returning a concrete `List<T>` invites callers to mutate state they don't own, creating bugs that are hard to trace back to the call site that broke the invariant.
scenario: A public SDK exposed `List<Order>` from `GetOrders()`; a consumer cleared and repopulated that list thinking it was a local copy, silently corrupting the SDK's internal cache until the API switched to IReadOnlyList<T>.

title: Catch specific exceptions, not Exception
description: Avoid broad `catch (Exception)` blocks that swallow errors — catch the specific types you can actually recover from, and log/rethrow the rest.
why: A broad `catch (Exception)` can swallow bugs you never meant to handle, leaving the program in a corrupted state that fails silently somewhere else later.
scenario: A batch import job wrapped its whole loop in catch (Exception), which silently swallowed a schema-mismatch error for weeks — thousands of records were skipped before a downstream report looked wrong enough for anyone to notice.

title: Use exception filters instead of catch-and-rethrow
description: An exception filter (`catch (Ex e) when (...)`) lets you conditionally handle an exception without catching and rethrowing, which preserves the original stack trace.
why: Catching and rethrowing resets the stack trace to the rethrow point, erasing exactly the information you need to find where the failure actually started.
scenario: A support team debugging an intermittent production crash kept losing the real stack trace because the code caught and rethrew; switching to an exception filter (`when` clause) for logging preserved the original trace and cut diagnosis time from days to minutes.

title: Favor pattern matching over long if/else chains
description: Use `is`/`switch` expressions to replace long `if`/`else if` chains that check types or values — it's more concise and the compiler can flag missing cases.
why: A `switch` expression is exhaustiveness-checked by the compiler, so a forgotten case gets flagged — an `if`/`else` chain gives you no such guarantee.
scenario: A billing engine's long if/else chain over subscription-tier strings missed a newly added "Enterprise" tier and silently fell through to the default price; a switch expression would have made the compiler flag the missing case.

title: Propagate and honor CancellationToken
description: Thread `CancellationToken` through async call chains and actually check/pass it through, rather than accepting the parameter and ignoring it.
why: A token that's accepted but never checked gives the illusion of cancellability while the operation keeps consuming resources for a caller that already gave up.
scenario: A search API accepted a CancellationToken but never passed it to the downstream Elasticsearch call; when users abandoned slow searches, the backend kept running the full query anyway, wasting cluster capacity under load.

title: Don't wrap I/O-bound work in Task.Run inside a web app
description: `Task.Run` just moves I/O-bound work to another thread-pool thread — it doesn't parallelize I/O and wastes a thread inside a request pipeline that's already async.
why: I/O-bound work isn't CPU-bound — moving it to another thread-pool thread doesn't make it finish faster, it just burns an extra thread for no benefit.
scenario: A web team wrapped a database call in Task.Run "to make it async"; that just moved the blocking wait to a different thread-pool thread, and the app still starved the pool under load exactly as before, now with extra overhead.

title: Use immutable collections for shared read-heavy state
description: Types like `ImmutableArray<T>` or `FrozenDictionary<T>` are a good fit for read-heavy, rarely-changing data accessed from multiple threads without locking.
why: Immutable data can be read from multiple threads with no locking at all, because nothing can change underneath a reader — that removes a whole category of race conditions.
scenario: A feature-flag service read a rarely-changing FrozenDictionary of flags from every request across dozens of threads with zero locking; the mutable Dictionary it replaced had needed a lock on every read and was a measurable contention point.

title: Use System.Text.Json source generation for AOT/perf-sensitive code
description: `[JsonSerializable]` source-generated serializers avoid reflection at startup and are required for trimmed/Native AOT apps to serialize reliably.
why: Reflection-based code paths are invisible to static trimming analysis, so trimming or Native AOT can silently strip members the reflection-based serializer still expects.
scenario: A CLI tool published with Native AOT for fast cold starts silently returned empty JSON for a type the reflection-based serializer needed but the trimmer had removed; switching to source-generated serializers fixed it and cut startup time further.

title: Validate arguments at public API boundaries
description: Use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` and similar guards at the start of public methods rather than letting bad state propagate deep into a call chain.
why: The earlier a bad argument is caught, the shorter the distance between cause and exception — validating deep in a call chain turns a one-line bug into a debugging session.
scenario: A shared library's `ProcessOrder(Order order)` didn't guard against a null order; the eventual NullReferenceException surfaced three call frames deep inside internal logic, turning a one-line check into a debugging session to trace back.

title: Don't use volatile as a substitute for synchronization
description: `volatile` only affects instruction reordering and visibility — it doesn't make compound operations (like increment) atomic; use proper locking for those.
why: `volatile` only guarantees visibility and ordering of a single read/write — a compound operation like `x++` is really a read-modify-write, and `volatile` does nothing to make those steps atomic.
scenario: A metrics counter marked volatile and incremented directly from multiple request threads silently under-counted events under load, because `x++` isn't atomic — volatile only guarantees visibility, not the read-modify-write.

title: Scope locks as tightly as possible
description: Keep the code inside a `lock`/`SemaphoreSlim` limited to the actual shared state being protected — don't hold a lock across unrelated or slow work.
why: Every extra statement held inside a lock extends how long every other thread waits for it, and holding it across slow work risks contention becoming a bottleneck or a deadlock.
scenario: A caching layer held a lock across a slow database refill call; under concurrent load every other request queued behind that one slow call, turning an occasional cache miss into a full app stall.

title: Profile before micro-optimizing
description: Apply low-level tricks like aggressive inlining only after profiling shows a specific hot path needs it — not by default across the codebase.
why: Intuition about hot paths is frequently wrong, and applying low-level tricks everywhere trades readability for performance gains that may not exist where you spent them.
scenario: A team spent a sprint adding aggressive-inlining hints across a codebase they assumed was CPU-bound; a profiler run afterward showed 90% of response time was actually a missing database index, and the optimization work moved nothing.

title: Version public API surface deliberately
description: Treat breaking changes to a public assembly/NuGet package's API as a major-version event, and avoid silently breaking consumers between minor versions.
why: A consumer upgrading a minor/patch version expects nothing to break — silently changing a public signature violates that contract and erodes trust in your versioning.
scenario: A NuGet package used internally by a dozen teams renamed a public method in what was tagged a patch release; every consuming team's build broke the same morning because the change should have been a major-version bump.

title: Use new syntax where it improves readability, not everywhere
description: Expression-bodied members and primary constructors read well for simple cases — don't reach for them reflexively where a normal method/constructor is clearer.
why: A language feature is a tool, not a mandate — using it where it doesn't actually clarify intent just adds unfamiliar syntax for the next reader to decode.
scenario: A code review flagged a primary constructor crammed with validation logic inline in the class declaration; reverting to a normal constructor with an explicit body made the validation readable instead of buried in the type signature.

title: Keep DTOs and records free of business logic
description: Data-carrying types should carry data — business rules belong in domain/application services, not inside a record or DTO.
why: Business logic embedded in a data-carrying type gets duplicated wherever that type is used, instead of living in one place every caller shares.
scenario: An order DTO grew a `CalculateDiscount()` method for convenience; six months later the same discount logic had been copy-pasted into three other services because nobody realized the DTO, not a shared service, owned the rule.

title: Enforce formatting and analyzers in CI
description: Run `dotnet format` and a Roslyn analyzer ruleset as a CI gate so style and common bug patterns are caught before a human reviews the PR.
why: A rule enforced only by convention gets skipped under deadline pressure — putting it in CI makes it non-negotiable instead of best-effort.
scenario: A team relied on "please run dotnet format before committing" as a README note; six months later half the codebase used tabs and half used spaces, because the convention was never actually enforced until it moved into a CI gate.

title: Watch for captive dependencies
description: Never inject a scoped/transient service directly into a singleton's constructor — it gets captured for the singleton's lifetime; resolve it from a scope/factory instead.
why: A singleton is constructed once, so a scoped dependency captured into it effectively becomes a singleton too — keeping stale state alive for the app's whole lifetime instead of per request.
scenario: A SaaS billing service injected a scoped DbContext directly into a singleton cache-warming service; the same DbContext instance stayed alive for the app's entire life, and change tracking corrupted itself within hours of deployment.

title: Keep middleware order intentional
description: Order the pipeline deliberately: exception handling and HTTPS redirection early, authentication after routing, endpoints last — order changes behavior, not just style.
why: Each middleware only sees what the ones before it pass along — putting authentication after the code that needs it means that code runs unauthenticated.
scenario: A fintech API put its authentication middleware after the endpoint routing that needed it; an internal admin endpoint was reachable without a valid token for a week before a security review caught the ordering bug.

title: Never expose Kestrel directly to the internet
description: Put a reverse proxy (IIS, Nginx, YARP) in front of Kestrel for TLS termination, request buffering, and basic hardening rather than exposing it publicly on its own.
why: Kestrel is optimized for speed, not for hardening against malformed requests or slow-loris style attacks — a reverse proxy is the layer built for that.
scenario: A startup exposed Kestrel directly to the internet to save the cost of a reverse proxy; a slow-loris style flood of half-open connections took the API down until IIS was put in front of it for hardening.

title: Use IOptionsMonitor for config that can change at runtime
description: Prefer `IOptionsMonitor<T>`/`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` over manually re-reading `IConfiguration` when settings can be reloaded without a restart.
why: Reading `IConfiguration` directly caches values at startup — code that needs a setting to update after a reload has to observe change notifications, which is what `IOptionsMonitor` provides.
scenario: An ops team needed to toggle a feature flag without redeploying; the service read IConfiguration once at startup and cached it, so the change never took effect until they switched the flag-reading code to IOptionsMonitor.

title: Return ProblemDetails for API errors
description: Use RFC 7807 `ProblemDetails` responses for API errors instead of ad-hoc error shapes, so every client can parse errors the same way.
why: A client integrating against many endpoints writes one error-parsing path instead of a different ad hoc shape per endpoint, which is exactly what a shared error contract buys you.
scenario: A partner integration team building against a logistics API had to write a different error parser for nearly every endpoint because each one shaped its error JSON differently; standardizing on ProblemDetails let them write one shared handler.

title: Keep controllers thin
description: A controller action should bind/validate input, call an application service, and map the result to a response — business logic belongs in the service layer.
why: Logic embedded in a controller can only be exercised through an HTTP request, making it slower and more awkward to unit test than a plain service class.
scenario: A claims-processing controller action grew to 200 lines of business rules mixed with HTTP concerns; testing a single pricing rule change meant standing up a full HTTP request, until the logic was extracted into a service the team could unit test directly.

title: Always resolve HttpClient via IHttpClientFactory
description: Inject `HttpClient` through `IHttpClientFactory` rather than instantiating it directly, to avoid DNS staleness and socket exhaustion issues.
why: A directly-instantiated `HttpClient` can hold a DNS entry indefinitely, so it never notices an endpoint's IP changing — the factory recycles the handler to avoid that.
scenario: A weather-data aggregator instantiated HttpClient directly per request; when the upstream provider rotated its DNS record during a failover, the app kept hammering the old dead IP because the handler never refreshed until it moved to IHttpClientFactory.

title: Configure Data Protection for multi-instance deployments
description: Persist and share the Data Protection key ring across instances — otherwise auth cookies and antiforgery tokens silently stop validating when requests land on a different instance.
why: Without a shared key ring, each instance encrypts with a different key, so a cookie issued by one instance fails to validate the moment a load balancer routes the next request elsewhere.
scenario: A retailer scaled a web app from one instance to three behind a load balancer; login sessions started randomly failing because each instance had its own Data Protection key ring, and a cookie issued by one instance failed validation on another.

title: Point liveness and readiness probes at the right checks
description: Liveness should only fail if the process itself is broken; readiness can fail while a healthy instance is still warming up — pointing an orchestrator at the wrong one causes unnecessary restarts.
why: An orchestrator restarts a container that fails liveness — pointing that at a naturally slow-to-warm-up check like readiness causes a restart loop instead of a graceful startup.
scenario: A Kubernetes-hosted service pointed its liveness probe at a readiness-style check that included a slow startup dependency; the pod kept getting killed and restarted in a loop during normal (slow) warm-up instead of just being marked not-ready.

title: Honor RequestAborted in long-running actions
description: Pass `HttpContext.RequestAborted` into downstream async calls so work actually stops when a client disconnects instead of running to completion for nothing.
why: Without propagating cancellation, work keeps running and consuming CPU and DB connections for a response nobody will ever receive.
scenario: A reporting endpoint kept running a five-minute aggregation query even after the requesting browser tab was closed; propagating HttpContext.RequestAborted into the query let the app cancel abandoned work and free up database connections.

title: Use structured logging, not string interpolation
description: Log with `ILogger<T>` message templates (`"User {UserId} logged in"`) rather than interpolated strings, so log fields stay queryable in your log sink.
why: An interpolated string bakes values into unstructured text so your log sink can't filter or aggregate by field — a template with named fields keeps that data queryable.
scenario: An on-call engineer needed to find every failed login for a specific user during an incident; because the team logged with `ILogger` message templates instead of interpolated strings, they filtered the log sink by the UserId field in seconds instead of grepping raw text.

title: Cache deliberately, not by default
description: Enable response/output caching and compression on endpoints that are actually cacheable — never cache mutable or per-user data without a correct cache key.
why: Caching mutable or per-user data with the wrong key silently serves one user's data to another — the failure mode isn't a crash, it's a data leak.
scenario: A news site enabled output caching broadly to speed up page loads, including a personalized "recommended for you" endpoint with the wrong cache key; users briefly saw each other's recommended articles until the cache scope was narrowed.

title: Version the API from day one
description: Decide on a versioning scheme (URL segment, header, media type) before you have external clients — retrofitting it afterward is far more disruptive.
why: Once external clients depend on a contract, any breaking change has to be coordinated with people outside your team — deciding the scheme upfront avoids retrofitting it under pressure.
scenario: A public API shipped with no versioning scheme decided on upfront; the first breaking change years later required coordinating a painful simultaneous migration with every external partner instead of just shipping a new version segment.

title: Scope CORS policies tightly
description: Configure CORS with the specific origins/methods/headers you need, and never combine `AllowAnyOrigin` with credentials — that combination is explicitly disallowed for good reason.
why: The browser's same-origin policy is one of the few defenses against a malicious site reading a logged-in user's data — combining `AllowAnyOrigin` with credentials effectively turns that defense off.
scenario: An internal tool enabled `AllowAnyOrigin` together with credentialed cookies to unblock a frontend dev quickly; a security audit flagged that any site on the internet could now make authenticated requests on a logged-in user's behalf.

title: Use WebApplicationFactory for integration tests
description: Test through the real pipeline — routing, filters, DI — with `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>` rather than only unit-testing controllers in isolation.
why: Unit-testing a controller in isolation never exercises routing, model binding, or filter ordering — bugs that only appear in the real pipeline go undetected until production.
scenario: A team's controller unit tests all passed, but a routing conflict between two endpoints only surfaced in production; switching integration tests to WebApplicationFactory caught the same conflict in CI by exercising the real pipeline.

title: Drain work on graceful shutdown
description: Use `IHostApplicationLifetime`/`IHostedService.StopAsync` to finish in-flight work during shutdown instead of letting the process hard-kill active requests.
why: A hard-killed process mid-request leaves the client with a half-finished response and can leave downstream state — a partially written record, an in-flight message — inconsistent.
scenario: A deployment pipeline hard-killed pods on every rollout; users mid-checkout got dropped connections and partially-charged orders until the service was updated to drain in-flight requests during IHostedService.StopAsync.

title: Put scheduled work in a hosted service
description: Background/scheduled work belongs in `IHostedService`/`BackgroundService`, not in fire-and-forget tasks kicked off from a controller action.
why: Fire-and-forget work kicked off from a request has no lifecycle tied to the app — it can be abandoned mid-run on shutdown with nothing tracking whether it completed.
scenario: A nightly cleanup job was kicked off as a fire-and-forget Task from a controller action; when the app recycled mid-run, the job silently stopped partway with no record it had failed, until it was moved into a proper BackgroundService.

title: Validate at the boundary and trust it after
description: Validate input via model binding and data annotations (or FluentValidation) at the API edge, and don't re-validate ad hoc scattered through downstream layers.
why: Re-validating the same input at every layer adds no safety once it's already checked once at the edge, and it multiplies the places a rule has to be kept in sync.
scenario: A team re-validated the same "email must be non-empty" rule in the controller, the service layer, and the repository; a rule change meant updating three places, and one was inevitably missed, until validation was consolidated at the API boundary.

title: Never block synchronously in request handling
description: Calling `.Result`, `Task.Wait()`, or blocking I/O inside a request handler starves the thread pool under concurrent load — keep the async chain unbroken.
why: The request thread pool is a shared, finite resource — one blocking call ties up a thread that could serve another request, and enough of them under load starves the whole app.
scenario: A checkout API called `.Result` on a payment-gateway call inside a request handler; under a flash-sale traffic spike the thread pool starved and unrelated endpoints across the same app started timing out.

title: Match API style to the surface's actual needs
description: Minimal APIs suit small, focused services; controller-based MVC suits larger surfaces that benefit from filters and conventions — pick per-service, not by habit.
why: Minimal APIs skip the filter/convention machinery MVC provides — using the wrong one means either fighting missing structure at scale or carrying unused ceremony for a small service.
scenario: A team defaulted every new service to full MVC with controllers and filters out of habit; a tiny internal health-check-aggregator service ended up carrying far more ceremony than a Minimal API would have needed for three routes.

title: Keep secrets out of appsettings.json in source control
description: Use user-secrets locally and a vault or managed identity in production rather than committing connection strings or API keys to `appsettings.json`.
why: Anything committed to source control is effectively permanent — even deleting it later leaves it recoverable from git history, which a vault or user-secrets never expose in the first place.
scenario: A contractor accidentally committed a production connection string in `appsettings.json`; even after it was deleted in a later commit, it remained recoverable from git history, forcing a full credential rotation.

title: Set explicit request limits and timeouts
description: Don't rely on framework defaults for request body size and timeouts on public-facing endpoints, especially ones accepting file uploads.
why: An endpoint with no upload size limit or timeout is an easy resource-exhaustion target — a single slow or oversized request can tie up a worker indefinitely.
scenario: A file-upload endpoint had no explicit body-size limit; a single malicious multi-gigabyte upload tied up a worker and disk space until explicit request limits were added to the pipeline.

title: Prefer constructor injection over [FromServices] for core dependencies
description: Constructor injection keeps a controller's dependencies visible in one place; reserve `[FromServices]` for occasional per-action needs.
why: A dependency hidden behind `[FromServices]` doesn't show up in the constructor, so understanding what a controller needs means reading every action instead of one signature.
scenario: A controller's dependencies were scattered across `[FromServices]` parameters on individual actions; a new engineer trying to understand what the controller needed had to read every action method instead of one constructor signature.

title: Propagate correlation IDs across service calls
description: Instrument with distributed tracing and correlation IDs so a single request can be followed end-to-end across services, not just within one service's logs.
why: In a system with more than one service, a single user request touches several independent log streams — without a shared ID there's no way to reconstruct what happened across them.
scenario: A checkout failure spanned three microservices; without a shared correlation ID, the on-call engineer had to manually cross-reference timestamps across three separate log streams to reconstruct what had actually happened to one user's request.

title: Use content negotiation instead of parallel endpoints per format
description: Let the `Accept` header drive response format via content negotiation rather than building separate endpoints for JSON, XML, etc.
why: Parallel endpoints per format duplicate the same logic behind different routes, so a bug fix or behavior change has to be applied in multiple places instead of once.
scenario: A public API maintained separate `/orders/json` and `/orders/xml` endpoints with duplicated logic; a bug fix was applied to one and forgotten in the other for months, until they were merged into one endpoint driven by the Accept header.

title: Apply rate limiting before you need it
description: Add rate-limiting middleware to public or expensive endpoints proactively, rather than reacting to the first abuse incident.
why: The first abuse incident is usually also the first time anyone notices the endpoint had no protection — by then it's already caused an outage or a cost spike.
scenario: A public signup endpoint had no rate limiting; a scraper hammered it with thousands of requests a minute until the database connection pool was exhausted, and rate-limiting middleware was added only after that outage.

title: Verify trimmed/AOT output, don't just trust the build
description: Reflection-based libraries can silently break under trimming or Native AOT — actually run the published output's test suite, not just the untrimmed build.
why: Trimming makes decisions from static analysis of what's reachable — reflection-based paths are invisible to that analysis and can be silently removed, so only the trimmed binary reveals the breakage.
scenario: A CLI tool passed all its unit tests against the normal build, then threw a missing-member exception the moment it was published as trimmed Native AOT, because a reflection-based path the trimmer had removed was still called at runtime.

title: Scope DbContext per request
description: Keep EF Core's `DbContext` scoped to a single request/unit of work — never share one instance across concurrent requests.
why: `DbContext` isn't thread-safe — sharing one instance across concurrent requests corrupts its internal change tracking in ways that produce confusing, intermittent errors.
scenario: A background job accidentally reused a single injected DbContext across two concurrent requests; change tracking got corrupted and started throwing intermittent "instance already tracked" errors that only reproduced under real concurrent load.

title: Add global exception-handling middleware
description: Use exception-handling middleware (or `IExceptionHandler`) so any unhandled exception returns a consistent, non-leaking error response instead of a raw stack trace.
why: An unhandled exception's default response can leak a stack trace and internal details — centralizing the handler guarantees every failure path returns the same safe, generic shape.
scenario: An API with no centralized exception handler leaked a full stack trace, including internal file paths, in a 500 response to an external partner; adding global exception-handling middleware normalized every failure path to the same safe response shape.

title: Load-test your health checks too
description: A health check that queries the database can itself become a bottleneck under load — include health/readiness endpoints in load testing, not just business endpoints.
why: A health check that queries the database adds load exactly when the system is already under load — if it becomes the bottleneck, it can get an orchestrator to kill healthy instances.
scenario: A team's readiness probe queried the primary database on every check; during a real traffic spike, the flood of health-check queries became the bottleneck that pushed the database over the edge and got Kubernetes to kill otherwise-healthy pods.

title: Apply Single Responsibility at the function level
description: A function should do one thing you can describe without using the word "and" — if you need "and", it's probably doing too much.
why: A function doing two things has two reasons to change — a fix or requirement change to one responsibility risks breaking the other, unrelated one.
scenario: A "ProcessOrder" method at a retailer validated input, charged the card, and sent the confirmation email all in one function; a change to the email template broke charge processing because the two unrelated concerns shared the same method.

title: Prefer guard clauses over deep nesting
description: Return early on invalid/edge cases at the top of a function instead of wrapping the main logic in nested conditionals.
why: Each level of nesting is another condition the reader has to hold in their head to follow what's actually running — guard clauses collapse that back to one path.
scenario: A loan-approval function nested five levels of if statements checking eligibility; a new engineer misread which branch a rule belonged to and introduced a bug that approved loans that should have been rejected, until the function was flattened with guard clauses.

title: Name things for what they represent
description: Choose names that describe intent (`GetActiveUsers()`) rather than implementation detail (`GetUsersWhereFlag1True()`).
why: A name reflecting only an implementation detail stops making sense the moment the implementation changes, even though what it represents hasn't.
scenario: A codebase had a method called `GetUsersWhereFlag1True()`; when the business later renamed what flag1 meant, the method name became actively misleading, and nobody wanted to touch it because its name no longer matched its purpose.

title: Keep functions short enough to review at a glance
description: If reviewing a function requires scrolling, it's a signal the function is doing more than one job and should be split.
why: Scrolling breaks the reader's ability to hold the whole function in view at once — the length itself is a signal it's outgrown a single responsibility.
scenario: A 300-line `CalculateInvoice` method required scrolling through three screens to review; splitting it into five named steps let a reviewer catch a tax-calculation bug in the third step that had been invisible in the wall of code before.

title: Comment the why, not the what
description: Well-named code already shows what it does; a comment earns its place by explaining a non-obvious constraint, workaround, or business rule.
why: A comment restating what the code does goes stale the moment the code changes; a comment explaining why can't be inferred from the code no matter how it's refactored.
scenario: A comment above a retry loop said "// retry the call" — restating the obvious code below it; a missing comment explaining that the retry count of exactly 3 matched a vendor's rate-limit reset window would have saved the next engineer from "simplifying" it away.

title: Write tests alongside the code, not after
description: Writing tests as you build a feature (or before, in TDD) catches design problems early instead of after the implementation has hardened around them.
why: Writing the test forces you to think through the interface and edge cases before the implementation hardens around a design that's awkward to test.
scenario: A team wrote the implementation of a discount-calculation feature first and tests after, under deadline pressure; the tests ended up validating whatever the code happened to do, including two bugs that shipped to production before anyone caught them.

title: Favor composition when you just need reuse
description: Reach for composition, not inheritance, when the goal is code reuse rather than modeling a genuine is-a relationship.
why: Inheritance couples a subclass to the base class's implementation details, so a change to the base can break subclasses in ways invisible at the call site.
scenario: An engineer made `PremiumUser` inherit from `RegularUser` to reuse its methods; a later change to RegularUser's base behavior broke PremiumUser in a way nobody expected, because the two were never truly an is-a relationship — composition would have avoided the coupling.

title: Optimize only what profiling shows is slow
description: Measure before optimizing — intuition about what's slow is frequently wrong, and premature optimization adds complexity for no measured benefit.
why: Optimizing the wrong thing adds complexity without moving the metric that matters — a profiler shows where the time actually goes, which is usually not where intuition points.
scenario: A team spent a week hand-optimizing a data-transformation function they assumed was the bottleneck; a profiler later showed 95% of the request time was actually a chatty network call the optimization never touched.

title: Wait for a third case before abstracting
description: Introduce a shared abstraction once you have at least two or three concrete cases that need it (rule of three) — not on the first hint of similarity.
why: An abstraction built from a single example tends to fit that one case perfectly and nothing else, forcing an awkward rewrite the moment a different second case appears.
scenario: A developer built a generic "ExportFormatter" abstraction after seeing just one CSV export use case; the first time a second, genuinely different PDF export needed it, the abstraction didn't fit and had to be reworked anyway.

title: Automate style instead of debating it in review
description: Let a linter/formatter enforce consistent style so reviewers spend their attention on correctness and design, not spacing and casing.
why: Debating spacing and casing in review spends reviewer attention on something a tool settles instantly, leaving less attention for the design and correctness issues only a human catches.
scenario: A team spent recurring review cycles debating tabs versus spaces and brace placement; once a formatter was wired into the pre-commit hook, those same review threads disappeared and reviewers started catching actual bugs instead.

title: Fail fast on bad input
description: Validate inputs and preconditions at the start of a function so invalid state is caught immediately instead of propagating and surfacing somewhere confusing later.
why: Invalid state left to propagate surfaces its symptom far from its cause, turning a one-line validation check into a multi-hour investigation.
scenario: A pricing function accepted a negative quantity without validation and let it flow four layers deep before finally producing a bizarre negative invoice total; failing fast at the entry point would have caught it in one line instead of a multi-hour trace.

title: Name magic values
description: Replace unexplained literals (`if (status == 3)`) with named constants or enums that describe what the value means.
why: `if (status == 3)` requires the reader to already know what 3 means — a named constant carries that meaning at the point of use instead of requiring lookup elsewhere.
scenario: A support ticket status check read `if (status == 3)`; nobody on the team could say from memory what 3 meant without checking the database, until it was replaced with a named `TicketStatus.Escalated` constant.

title: Keep side effects explicit and localized
description: A method named `GetX` shouldn't also mutate shared state or write to a database — separate queries from commands.
why: A method that looks like a pure query but secretly mutates state breaks the reader's ability to reason about what calling it does, and makes reordering or caching calls unsafe.
scenario: A method named `GetActiveSubscriptions()` also silently updated a "last checked" timestamp on every call; a caching layer that assumed the method was a pure read started producing stale, inconsistent timestamps once it began calling it less often.

title: Delete dead code instead of commenting it out
description: Version control already preserves history — commented-out code just adds noise and eventually goes stale and misleading.
why: Commented-out code reads as if it might still matter, wasting the next reader's time deciding whether it's safe to ignore — version control already remembers it if it's ever needed again.
scenario: A codebase had a block of commented-out authentication logic sitting untouched for two years; a new engineer wasted an afternoon deciding whether it was safe to delete before finally confirming via git blame it had been dead since a refactor that long ago.

title: Document what the code genuinely can't show
description: Reserve a README or doc comment for things a reader can't infer from the code itself (deployment steps, non-obvious tradeoffs) — don't restate the obvious.
why: A doc that restates the code is a second thing to keep in sync and go stale — it earns its place only where the code genuinely can't express the information itself.
scenario: A deployment required a manual database migration step that wasn't written down anywhere; a release went out without it and broke in production, until the step was documented in a README the code itself could never have conveyed.

title: Handle errors where there's enough context to act
description: Don't catch an exception just to make a method appear not to throw — handle it where the code actually knows what recovery looks like.
why: Catching an exception where you don't know how to recover just delays the failure — better to let it propagate to a layer with enough context to decide what recovery looks like.
scenario: A low-level file-reading helper caught and swallowed every IOException just so it wouldn't "look like it throws"; the caller never learned the read had failed and silently processed an empty result, until the exception was allowed to propagate to a layer that actually knew how to retry or alert.

title: Name tests after behavior, not implementation
description: A test named "returns 404 when the id doesn't exist" survives a refactor that a test named "Test_Method1" doesn't.
why: A test named after an implementation detail breaks or gets deleted the moment that implementation is refactored, even when the behavior it protected hasn't changed.
scenario: A refactor renamed an internal helper method, and every test named `Test_Method1` through `Test_Method7` broke even though none of the actual behavior had changed; tests named after behavior like "returns 404 when the id doesn't exist" survived the same refactor untouched.

title: Avoid clever one-liners over clear code
description: Nested ternaries and dense one-liners save a few lines but cost readers time every time they're read — prefer the clearer version.
why: Saving a few lines at write time costs every future reader time decoding it — code is read far more often than it's written.
scenario: A nested nine-way ternary computing shipping cost passed code review without comment because the author understood it; the next engineer who had to change one branch spent an hour just parsing the expression before making a one-line fix.

title: Treat warnings as errors in CI
description: An ignored compiler or linter warning is effectively a bug report nobody reads — fail the build on new warnings instead.
why: A warning nobody's required to act on gets ignored indefinitely until the signal is buried in noise — treating it as a build failure keeps it acted on immediately.
scenario: A build had accumulated 400 ignored compiler warnings over two years; one of them turned out to be a real null-dereference bug that shipped to production, and the team only started catching these again once CI was configured to fail on any new warning.

title: Keep environment-specific values out of code
description: Configuration that differs by environment belongs in config/environment variables, not hardcoded constants recompiled per environment.
why: A hardcoded environment-specific value forces a rebuild to change environments and risks the wrong value shipping to the wrong one by mistake.
scenario: A staging API URL was hardcoded as a constant and compiled into the binary; a release accidentally shipped the staging URL to production because the value never got updated in the fixed build, instead of being read from environment configuration.

title: Design operations to be idempotent where practical
description: Anything that might be retried — a message handler, a migration, a webhook receiver — should be safe to run more than once with the same effect.
why: Anything that can be retried eventually will be — a network blip, a redelivered message — and a non-idempotent handler run twice produces a duplicated or corrupted side effect.
scenario: A payment-webhook handler wasn't idempotent; a network retry from the payment provider caused the same order to be charged twice, and the fix was to make the handler safely re-runnable using the provider's idempotency key.

title: Make dependencies explicit via injection
description: Pass dependencies in rather than reaching for hidden global/static state — it makes the code's requirements visible and testable.
why: Hidden static state can be mutated from anywhere in the codebase, making a test's outcome depend on what ran before it instead of only its own inputs.
scenario: A reporting module reached for a static `DateTime.Now` and a static logger scattered throughout its code; tests that needed to control the current date couldn't, because nothing about the module's real dependencies was visible or injectable from outside.

title: Keep pull requests small and focused
description: A PR scoped to one logical change is easier to review thoroughly and easier to revert cleanly if it causes a problem.
why: Review quality degrades sharply as diff size grows — a reviewer skimming a huge change catches far less than one reading a focused, small one.
scenario: A 2,000-line PR that refactored authentication and added a new feature in the same diff got a shallow rubber-stamp approval after sitting unreviewed for a week; splitting it into two focused PRs later became the team's standard after a bug slipped through in that mega-PR.

title: Record the why behind unusual decisions
description: Capture the reasoning for a non-obvious technical choice in an ADR or commit message — otherwise it gets re-litigated or reverted by someone who didn't know why it was done that way.
why: Without a record of the reasoning, a future engineer who doesn't understand why an unusual decision was made is likely to "fix" it back to the more obvious approach that was already tried and rejected.
scenario: A team saw a deliberately "non-idiomatic" retry pattern in the codebase and reverted it back to the obvious approach during a cleanup pass, reintroducing a race condition it had originally been written to avoid — a one-line ADR comment would have prevented the regression.

title: Don't force a shared abstraction onto coincidental similarity
description: DRY applies to actual duplicated business rules, not code that merely looks alike today but represents different concerns that will diverge.
why: Code that looks alike today but represents different business concerns will diverge over time — merging it into one abstraction now just means untangling it again later under pressure.
scenario: Two teams merged their superficially similar "validate an email" and "validate a username" logic into one shared function to avoid duplication; six months later the two rules had diverged in every requirement, and untangling the shared abstraction took longer than the duplication ever would have.

title: Prefer strongly-typed models over dynamic/dictionaries
description: Passing `dynamic` or loosely-typed dictionaries between layers defers type errors to runtime — a proper model catches them at compile time.
why: A typo in a dictionary key or a dynamic property only fails when that code path actually runs — a compiler catches the same mistake before the code ever ships.
scenario: An integrations team passed loosely-typed dictionaries between services for flexibility; a renamed key in one upstream service silently broke a downstream consumer at runtime, a bug a strongly-typed model would have caught at compile time.

title: Reserve Error-level logs for things that need attention
description: Log expected/handled conditions at Info or Warning — flooding Error-level logs with routine events trains people to ignore alerts.
why: If routine, expected conditions log at Error, the alert channel trains everyone to ignore it — the one log that actually needs attention gets lost in the noise of ones that don't.
scenario: An on-call rotation got paged every night for an Error-level log that turned out to be a routine retry succeeding on its second attempt; once it was downgraded to Warning, the real Error-level alert that mattered stood out immediately during the next actual outage.

title: Write for the reader debugging an incident at 2am
description: Optimize code clarity for the stressed reader under time pressure, not for the person who already understands it because they wrote it.
why: The person reading your code under incident pressure has none of the context you had while writing it — clarity you skip to save time now costs someone else far more later.
scenario: A senior engineer wrote a clever one-liner they understood perfectly at the time; six months later, debugging a 2am outage, a different engineer lost twenty minutes just decoding what that one line did before they could even start diagnosing the actual bug.

title: Automate what discipline alone won't sustain
description: Formatting, dependency updates, and changelog entries should be automated — relying on every developer to remember them consistently doesn't scale.
why: A manual step that depends on every developer remembering it every time will eventually be forgotten — automating it removes the dependency on memory entirely.
scenario: A team relied on each developer remembering to bump the changelog by hand; entries were missing from half the releases until the changelog generation was automated from commit messages instead.

title: Refactor incrementally as you touch code
description: Apply the boy scout rule — leave code a little better each time you're in it — instead of waiting for a big-bang rewrite that rarely gets scheduled.
why: Waiting for a dedicated rewrite lets debt keep compounding in the meantime, and a big-bang rewrite competing against feature work rarely gets prioritized or scheduled.
scenario: A payments module had been "scheduled for a rewrite" for two years while feature work kept taking priority; a team that instead cleaned up whatever file they touched, a little at a time, had visibly less debt in the same module a year later.

title: Let tooling catch style, humans catch design
description: Automate formatting and linting so reviewers spend their limited attention on correctness, design, and edge cases instead of spacing and casing.
why: Every minute a reviewer spends on spacing is a minute not spent catching a design flaw or a bug — automation is strictly better at the mechanical part.
scenario: A team's PR threads used to be dominated by comments about brace placement and trailing commas; after wiring a linter into CI, reviewers redirected that same attention to a genuine race condition in the next PR that style debates had been crowding out.

title: Keep pull requests small
description: Review quality drops sharply on large diffs — aim for PRs under a few hundred changed lines where the change is separable.
why: A reviewer's attention and thoroughness both drop as diff size grows, so a large PR gets a shallower review exactly when it has more surface area to miss something in.
scenario: A 1,500-line PR bundling a database migration, a UI change, and a bug fix got a shallow same-day approval; a smaller, focused version of the same work a month later caught a real off-by-one error the big PR's reviewer had simply skimmed past.

title: Explain why in the PR description
description: The diff already shows what changed — the description should carry the reasoning, the alternatives considered, and any tradeoffs made.
why: The diff shows what changed but not what alternatives were considered or rejected — without that, a reviewer can't tell whether a questionable-looking choice was deliberate.
scenario: A reviewer saw a PR replace a well-known library with a hand-rolled implementation and nearly blocked it as unnecessary; the description explained the library had an unresolved CVE, which the diff alone never would have conveyed.

title: Actually run non-trivial changes, don't just read the diff
description: For anything beyond a trivial change, check the branch out and exercise it — some bugs are invisible in a diff view.
why: Some bugs — a broken interaction, a layout issue, an exception under real data — simply don't show up by reading code, only by exercising it.
scenario: A reviewer approved a form-validation change purely by reading the diff; a co-worker who actually ran the branch found the submit button was silently disabled on Safari, a bug invisible in the code itself.

title: Separate blocking feedback from nitpicks
description: Prefix optional suggestions (e.g. "nit:") so the author can tell at a glance what must be addressed before merge versus what's a take-it-or-leave-it idea.
why: Without a clear signal, an author can't tell whether a suggestion is something they must address before merging, which either stalls the PR or causes real feedback to be ignored.
scenario: An author saw ten review comments with no priority signal and assumed all ten were blocking, delaying the merge by two days; the team adopted a "nit:" prefix convention afterward so authors could tell required fixes from optional ones at a glance.

title: Review test coverage, not just production code
description: Untested logic is a gap in the review itself — check that new behavior has tests, not only that the implementation looks right.
why: Correct-looking implementation code with no test is unverified — the review is incomplete if it only checks that the code looks right instead of that it's proven right.
scenario: A PR added a new discount-calculation path with clean, correct-looking code and zero tests; it shipped a rounding bug that a single missing test case would have caught, which became the team's case for requiring test coverage as part of review.

title: Explain your reasoning when responding to feedback
description: Reply with why you made a change (or didn't) rather than just pushing a fix silently — it lets the reviewer verify intent, not just the diff.
why: A silent fix doesn't tell the reviewer whether their concern was actually understood and addressed, or just changed in a way that happens to look different.
scenario: An author pushed a fix to a review comment without any explanation; the reviewer couldn't tell if their actual concern (a race condition) was addressed or if the diff just happened to look different, and had to ask before approving.

title: Don't rubber-stamp what you didn't read
description: An approval is a statement you'd stand behind the change — approving without understanding it defeats the purpose of review.
why: An approval signals to the team that the change was actually vetted — approving without reading it means that signal no longer means anything.
scenario: A reviewer approved a large refactor without reading it closely, assuming a teammate would catch anything real; a subtle authorization bug shipped to production because everyone assumed someone else's approval meant it had actually been checked.

title: Set a review turnaround expectation
description: A same-business-day SLA for first review keeps PRs from stalling and authors from context-switching away and losing momentum.
why: A PR sitting unreviewed for days causes the author to context-switch to other work, and picking the change back up later costs more than the review itself would have.
scenario: A PR sat unreviewed for four days while its author moved on to other work; by the time it finally got reviewed, the author had lost the context and needed a full afternoon just to remember what the change did before responding to feedback.

title: Review for security, not just function
description: Check input validation, authorization checks, and secret handling explicitly during review — these are easy to miss when scanning only for correctness.
why: Security issues rarely announce themselves as broken behavior — a missing authorization check works fine for every legitimate user and only fails for an attacker, so it has to be actively looked for.
scenario: A PR added a new admin endpoint that worked correctly for every legitimate test case the author tried; a reviewer specifically checking for authorization caught that it had no role check at all, something functional testing alone would never have surfaced.

title: Ask before asserting when unsure
description: If an approach looks wrong but you might be missing context, ask a question first rather than stating it's incorrect outright.
why: Stating something as wrong when you're actually missing context puts the author on the defensive and wastes a round-trip correcting a false alarm — a question gets the same information without the friction.
scenario: A reviewer flatly stated an approach was "wrong" in a comment; it turned out the author had already ruled out the reviewer's preferred approach for a reason not visible in the diff, and the blunt phrasing cost a defensive back-and-forth that a question would have avoided.

title: Use draft PRs for early direction feedback
description: Open a draft PR to get feedback on approach before investing in a fully polished implementation that might need to change direction.
why: Getting feedback on approach before the implementation is polished means a change in direction costs a partial rewrite instead of a full one.
scenario: An engineer opened a draft PR halfway through a risky refactor to get early feedback on direction; a reviewer flagged a fundamentally different approach before the engineer had sunk two more days into polishing the wrong design.

title: Flag technical debt even in working code
description: Call out a missing index, an N+1 query, or an unbounded cache even if the PR functions correctly today — it will cost more to fix later.
why: A working PR with a hidden N+1 query or unbounded cache looks fine until it's the code path under production load — surfacing it while it's fresh is far cheaper than rediscovering it during an incident.
scenario: A reviewer noticed a new query had no index on a growing table but approved it anyway since it worked fine in testing; six months later that exact query was the slow one paging on-call during a traffic spike.

title: Make comments actionable
description: "This could be clearer" is less useful than a concrete suggested rewording the author can accept or push back on directly.
why: A vague comment leaves the author guessing what would actually satisfy it, often producing back-and-forth that a concrete suggestion would have avoided entirely.
scenario: A comment just said "this could be clearer" with no specifics; the author guessed at three different rewrites before the reviewer finally proposed the actual wording they had in mind, a round-trip a concrete suggestion would have skipped.

title: Move design debates out of the comment thread
description: When a review comment turns into a design discussion, take it to a call and summarize the resolution back in the PR for the record.
why: A design disagreement playing out over async comments takes far longer to resolve than a synchronous conversation, and clutters the PR history with a debate rather than a decision.
scenario: A caching-strategy disagreement dragged across forty back-and-forth PR comments over two days; moving it to a 15-minute call resolved it immediately, and a one-line summary comment on the PR preserved the decision for anyone reading it later.

title: Require a reviewer with context on the affected area
description: Route reviews to someone who understands the area being changed, not just whoever is fastest to approve.
why: A reviewer unfamiliar with the affected area can check syntax and style but is far less likely to catch a change that violates an assumption the rest of that area depends on.
scenario: A PR touching the tenant-isolation logic in a multi-tenant database layer was approved quickly by whoever was free, not by anyone who owned that area; a subtle cross-tenant data leak shipped that a reviewer familiar with the isolation invariants would have caught immediately.

title: Scrutinize test assertions as carefully as the implementation
description: A test that can never fail provides false confidence and is arguably worse than having no test at all.
why: A test with a weak or missing assertion passes regardless of whether the code is correct — that's a worse outcome than no test because it looks like coverage that isn't real.
scenario: A test for a refund calculation asserted only `result != null`; the underlying calculation was wrong for weeks, and the test passed the entire time because its assertion could never actually fail.

title: Gate human review behind CI status
description: Let build, test, and static analysis results pass before spending reviewer time — don't have humans catch what automation already would.
why: Spending reviewer time on a change that fails a basic build or test wastes the one resource CI doesn't need — a human's attention.
scenario: A reviewer spent twenty minutes reading through a PR before noticing the build itself was failing; after that, the team required CI to pass green before a human review was even requested, so reviewer time was never spent on something automation would've caught first.

title: Propose an alternative when you disagree
description: Pair disagreement with a concrete alternative and its tradeoff, rather than only flagging that something is wrong.
why: Flagging something as wrong without an alternative leaves the author guessing what you'd actually accept — a concrete counter-proposal turns the review into a decision instead of a stall.
scenario: A reviewer commented "this caching approach won't scale" with no alternative; the PR stalled for a week until they came back with a concrete suggestion — using a distributed cache instead — which the author implemented the same day.

title: Re-review promptly after changes land
description: A PR that addressed feedback deserves the same turnaround as the original review — don't let follow-ups sit longer than the first pass.
why: A follow-up round that sits as long as the first pass doubles the PR's total time in review, and the author's context on the change has already faded by then.
scenario: An author addressed a reviewer's feedback and pushed a fix, then waited three more days for a re-review while their context on the change faded; the team's SLA change to treat follow-up reviews the same as first-pass reviews cut that wait to hours.

title: Check consistency with existing codebase patterns
description: New code that works in isolation but diverges from established conventions creates long-term maintenance cost — flag it during review.
why: Code that works but diverges from the codebase's conventions means every future reader has to learn a second pattern just to understand that one file.
scenario: A new engineer wrote a perfectly functional data-access layer that didn't follow the repository pattern the rest of the codebase used; the reviewer flagged it not as broken but as inconsistent, saving every future reader from having to learn a second pattern for one file.

title: Call out good decisions, not only problems
description: Positive feedback in review reinforces the practices you want repeated, not just corrects the ones you don't.
why: Feedback that only ever corrects gives no signal about what to keep doing — naming a good decision reinforces the behavior you actually want repeated.
scenario: A reviewer only ever left comments pointing out problems; a teammate who'd made a genuinely clean refactor got no acknowledgment at all, and started wondering whether their reviews were only ever going to be corrections instead of also recognizing good calls.

title: Don't review while rushed or fatigued
description: A distracted 5-minute review catches less than a focused 15-minute one done later — schedule review time deliberately.
why: A rushed pass catches surface issues but misses the subtler ones that actually cause incidents — a distracted five minutes isn't a substitute for a focused fifteen.
scenario: A reviewer approved a PR in a rushed five minutes between meetings; a bug in the error-handling path they skimmed past caused a production incident a week later that a focused fifteen-minute review would very likely have caught.

title: Check edge cases, not just the happy path
description: Confirm empty input, null, timeout, and partial-failure scenarios are handled — these are the cases most often missing from a first draft.
why: The happy path is what got tested during development; the edge cases — empty input, timeout, partial failure — are exactly the ones most likely to have been missed.
scenario: A PR handled the happy path for a file upload cleanly but never considered what happened on a zero-byte file or a timed-out connection; a reviewer who specifically asked "what happens on empty input?" caught both gaps before merge.

title: Flag missing documentation on public APIs
description: Undocumented public interfaces are cheaper to fix during review than after other teams start depending on the undocumented behavior.
why: An undocumented public interface is easy to fix while the author still has full context — once other teams start depending on its undocumented behavior, changing it becomes a breaking change.
scenario: A team shipped an internal SDK method with no documented behavior for a null parameter; another team guessed wrong about what it did, built against that wrong assumption, and the eventual fix became a breaking change instead of a five-minute doc fix during the original review.

title: Keep a shared checklist for recurring review concerns
description: A written checklist (security, migrations, breaking changes) means review quality doesn't depend entirely on one reviewer's memory.
why: Relying on one reviewer's memory means review quality varies by who's assigned — a written checklist makes the bar consistent regardless of who's reviewing.
scenario: Whether a reviewer remembered to check for a missing database index or a breaking API change varied entirely by who was assigned; adopting a shared review checklist for migrations and breaking changes made review quality consistent regardless of who reviewed.

title: Treat review feedback as data about the codebase, not criticism
description: Recurring feedback usually points to a codebase or process gap worth fixing at the source, not just a personal correction.
why: If the same category of mistake keeps showing up across different authors, the problem is more likely a codebase or process gap than a string of individual oversights.
scenario: Three different authors independently made the same off-by-one mistake in pagination logic over two months; the team realized the pattern pointed to a confusing shared helper function, not three unrelated mistakes, and fixed the helper instead of just flagging each instance.

title: Don't approve past unresolved must-fix comments
description: If a blocking comment truly can't be addressed before merge, track it as an explicit fast-follow ticket rather than silently approving over it.
why: A "must-fix" comment that gets silently approved over sets a precedent that blocking feedback is optional, which erodes the entire point of marking something as blocking.
scenario: A reviewer left a "must-fix" comment about a missing null check, then approved the PR anyway under deadline pressure without it being addressed; the null reference exception it warned about hit production a week later, exactly as flagged and ignored.

title: Rotate reviewers across the team
description: Spreading review responsibility avoids both a single-person bottleneck and knowledge concentrating in just one reviewer.
why: Concentrating review in one person creates both a bottleneck when they're unavailable and a single point of failure for institutional knowledge about that area.
scenario: One senior engineer reviewed nearly every PR touching the payments module for years; when they went on leave, PRs in that area stalled for a week because no one else had built up the context to review them confidently.

title: Require domain sign-off for high-risk changes
description: Changes touching auth, payments, or migrations deserve a second reviewer or a specific owner's sign-off beyond the standard review.
why: A generalist reviewer can miss a subtlety in auth or payment logic that's obvious to someone who owns that domain — the blast radius of getting it wrong justifies the extra step.
scenario: A schema migration touching the primary users table was approved by a single generalist reviewer under normal process; it silently dropped a column still read by a reporting job, an issue the database team's sign-off process was specifically designed to catch for high-risk changes.

title: Choose a branching model deliberately
description: Pick trunk-based development, GitHub flow, or Git flow based on your actual release cadence, and document the choice — don't let it emerge by accident.
why: A branching model that emerges by accident usually reflects whatever the last person needed, not what actually fits your release cadence, and it's harder to change once habits form around it.
scenario: A startup's branching model had just evolved organically from whatever the founding engineer did first; once they hired a team shipping multiple times a day, they formally adopted trunk-based development and documented it, ending recurring confusion about when to branch versus commit to main.

title: Keep feature branches short-lived
description: Branches open for days, not weeks, minimize merge conflicts and drift from `main`, and keep code review scoped to a reviewable size.
why: The longer a branch lives, the further it drifts from `main`, and the more likely its eventual merge produces conflicts that are hard to resolve correctly.
scenario: A feature branch for a checkout redesign stayed open for six weeks while main kept moving; merging it back produced over 40 conflicting files, a mess a team that merged every two days would never have hit.

title: Sync from main frequently, not once at the end
description: Merge or rebase `main` into your feature branch regularly so conflicts surface early and in small pieces, not all at once before the PR.
why: A conflict caught early is a few lines in a file you just touched — the same conflict caught at the end of a long branch can span dozens of files you no longer remember the context for.
scenario: An engineer worked in isolation on a branch for two weeks without syncing main; the eventual merge surfaced a conflict spanning a dozen files they no longer remembered the context for, instead of the handful of small, fresh conflicts daily syncing would have produced.

title: Use feature flags instead of long-lived branches
description: Merge incomplete work behind a feature flag so `main` stays current and the branch stays short-lived, rather than isolating work for weeks.
why: Code hidden behind a flag still merges and gets tested against `main` continuously — code isolated on a long branch doesn't get that integration signal until the very end.
scenario: A team kept a redesign isolated on a branch for a month waiting for it to be "done"; a team that instead merged the same work behind a feature flag caught an integration bug with a concurrent billing change on day two instead of at the end.

title: Protect main with required checks and reviews
description: No direct pushes to `main`/release branches — require passing CI and at least one review before merge.
why: Without required checks, a single bad direct push can break `main` for everyone else pulling from it, with no review having had the chance to catch it first.
scenario: An engineer pushed a config typo directly to main during an emergency fix, breaking the build for everyone else pulling that morning; after that the team required CI and one review before any merge to main, even for hotfixes.

title: Name branches for intent
description: A branch name like `fix/checkout-timeout-bug` tells a teammate what it's for; `jsmith-patch-1` tells them nothing.
why: A name like `jsmith-patch-1` gives a teammate scanning the branch list zero information about what it's for or whether it's safe to ignore or delete.
scenario: A repo accumulated branches named `jsmith-patch-1` and `temp2`; nobody could tell from the branch list what was safe to delete, until the team adopted `fix/checkout-timeout-bug`-style names that explained themselves.

title: Match merge strategy to branch lifespan
description: Squash-merge short, tidy feature branches for a clean history; use merge commits for long-running branches where the individual commit history matters.
why: Squashing a long-running branch throws away individual commit history that might matter for bisecting a regression, but keeping every WIP commit from a short branch just adds noise.
scenario: A long-running branch with months of incremental commits got squash-merged into one giant commit; when a regression needed to be bisected weeks later, the team had lost the individual commit history that would have pinpointed exactly which change introduced it.

title: Never force-push a shared branch without coordinating
description: Rewriting history that others have already pulled causes silent divergence and lost work unless everyone knows to re-sync.
why: Rewriting history that others have already pulled leaves their local branch pointing at commits that no longer exist upstream, and their next pull silently diverges instead of erroring clearly.
