scenario: An engineer force-pushed a rebased shared feature branch without telling the two teammates also working on it; their next pull silently diverged from commits that no longer existed upstream, and they lost half a day of work reconciling it.

title: Cut release branches only when you need to stabilize
description: Reserve release branches for when `main` needs to keep moving while a release is being stabilized — don't default to one for every change.
why: Cutting a release branch for every change adds merge and maintenance overhead with no actual benefit when `main` isn't under active stabilization pressure.
scenario: A team cut a release branch for every single change out of habit; the overhead of merging fixes into a dozen open release branches consumed more time than the one release branch they actually needed during real stabilization.

title: Keep commit messages clear regardless of convention
description: Whether or not you adopt Conventional Commits for tooling, every commit message should explain what changed and why in a way a future reader can act on.
why: `git blame` and `git log` are often the only record of why a line changed — a vague message means that context is gone the moment the author forgets it.
scenario: A commit message simply said "fix bug"; six months later, tracking down why a specific validation rule existed meant re-deriving the reasoning from scratch instead of reading a commit message that explained it in one sentence.

title: Tag releases explicitly
description: Tag the exact commit that shipped (`v1.4.0`) rather than relying on branch names or memory to reconstruct what's in production.
why: A branch name keeps moving forward with new commits, so without a tag there's no fixed, unambiguous reference to what was actually deployed at a given time.
scenario: A production incident needed to confirm exactly what code was live; without a `v1.4.0` tag, the team had to reconstruct the deployed commit from deploy logs and guesswork instead of checking out one unambiguous reference.

title: Delete merged branches promptly
description: A branch list cluttered with long-merged branches makes it harder to see what's actually still in flight.
why: A branch list cluttered with long-dead branches makes it harder to tell which of the remaining ones represent real, active work.
scenario: A repository accumulated 200 long-merged branches over a year; new engineers couldn't tell which of the remaining branches represented real in-flight work until the team started deleting branches immediately after merge.

title: Hotfix from the deployed tag, not from a moved-on main
description: If `main` has advanced past what's in production, branch the hotfix from the release tag so you don't accidentally ship unrelated in-flight changes.
why: Branching a hotfix from a `main` that's advanced past production risks shipping unrelated in-flight changes as a side effect of the fix.
scenario: A hotfix branched from a main that had already advanced three unrelated feature commits past production; the "quick fix" release accidentally shipped one of those in-progress features half-finished, because it wasn't branched from the deployed tag.

title: Route even tiny fixes through the same PR process
description: Direct commits to `main`, even for "trivial" changes, skip the review and CI gate that exists precisely to catch small mistakes.
why: A "trivial" direct commit skips exactly the review and CI gate that exists to catch the small mistakes that look trivial but aren't.
scenario: An engineer pushed a "one-line" config change directly to main to save time; it turned out to be a typo that broke production, exactly the kind of small mistake the normal PR and CI gate exists to catch.

title: Rebase before merging when it's safe
description: Rebasing a feature branch onto `main` before merge keeps history linear and readable, as long as the branch isn't shared with others mid-rebase.
why: A linear history is easier to read and bisect than one tangled with merge commits from every sync — rebasing gets you that as long as the branch isn't shared mid-rebase.
scenario: A feature branch with a tangle of merge commits from weekly syncs was nearly impossible to bisect when a regression appeared; a team that rebased cleanly before merging kept a linear history that made the same investigation take minutes.

title: Keep branches about code, not environment
description: Environment-specific configuration belongs in config/environment variables, not in separate long-lived branches per environment.
why: A long-lived per-environment branch inevitably drifts from the others, so the same code ends up subtly different across environments instead of identical with different config.
scenario: A team maintained separate long-lived `staging-branch` and `prod-branch` branches for environment config; the two drifted apart over months until code behaved differently in each environment for reasons nobody could fully explain, until config moved to environment variables instead.

title: Keep commits at one logical change each
description: Consistent commit granularity keeps `git bisect` and selective reverts useful — a commit mixing three unrelated changes defeats both.
why: A commit mixing unrelated changes can't be bisected or reverted independently — you're forced to take all of it or none of it.
scenario: A single commit mixed a database migration, a bug fix, and an unrelated refactor; when the migration alone needed to be reverted after a production issue, the team couldn't do it without also reverting the unrelated refactor bundled into the same commit.

title: Avoid long-lived integration branches
description: A branch that diverges from `main` for weeks before merging recreates the same merge pain trunk-based development is meant to avoid.
why: An integration branch that diverges for weeks recreates the exact merge pain — stale assumptions, conflicting changes — that trunk-based development exists to avoid.
scenario: An "integration branch" for a major redesign stayed open for two months collecting changes from three engineers; merging it back recreated exactly the stale-assumption conflicts trunk-based development was adopted to avoid in the first place.

title: Run CI on the branch, not just after merge
description: Catch breakage before it lands in `main` by requiring the branch's own CI run to pass, not relying on post-merge detection.
why: Catching breakage after it's already in `main` means everyone else pulling `main` inherits the broken state until it's fixed.
scenario: A team only ran CI after merging to main; a broken build sat in main for four hours before anyone noticed, breaking every other engineer's pull, until CI was required to pass on the branch itself before merge.

title: Document conflict resolution for generated files
description: Lock files and generated migrations conflict often and naive resolution can silently corrupt them — write down the correct resolution procedure.
why: A lock file or generated migration resolved by guesswork can silently produce a corrupted file that looks valid but breaks the build or schema in a way that's hard to trace back to the merge.
scenario: Two engineers resolved a conflicting lock-file merge by guessing which version to keep; the resulting file looked valid but silently broke a transitive dependency version, a corruption that a documented resolution procedure would have prevented.

title: Open draft PRs early for visibility
description: A draft PR against a feature branch shares progress and invites early comment without requesting a full review yet.
why: Early visibility catches a wrong direction while it's still cheap to change, instead of after the implementation is fully built out.
scenario: An engineer built out a full redesign in isolation for a week before opening a PR; a reviewer immediately flagged a fundamentally different expected approach that an early draft PR would have surfaced on day one instead of after a week of wasted work.

title: Keep main always deployable
description: Trunk-based development's actual point is that `main` can be deployed at any time — treat any state that breaks that as an incident, not a style preference.
why: The entire value of trunk-based development depends on `main` being deployable at any moment — treating a break as routine instead of an incident erodes that guarantee for everyone.
scenario: A team treated a broken main as routine — "it'll get fixed eventually" — and left it red for two days; once they started treating any break as a real incident requiring an immediate fix or revert, main actually stayed deployable at all times as trunk-based development requires.

title: Prefer revert over force-push for a bad deployed commit
description: Reverting a merged, deployed commit is safer and more auditable than force-pushing `main` to erase it.
why: A revert is a new commit anyone can see and audit; a force-push erases history, which is much harder to reason about after the fact and riskier if others have already pulled.
scenario: A bad commit reached main and broke production; the on-call engineer force-pushed main to erase it, which silently diverged everyone else's already-pulled local copies, versus a revert commit that would have been visible and safe for everyone to pull.

title: Balance branch protection against review latency
description: Required checks and reviews should catch real risk — too many gates on every branch makes even trivial fixes take hours to land.
why: Every required check adds latency to every merge — too many gates on low-risk branches makes even a one-line fix take hours, pushing people toward workarounds that bypass the process entirely.
scenario: A one-line typo fix required five separate approvals and three CI stages to merge, taking four hours; the team scoped down required checks so low-risk changes could land quickly while high-risk paths kept the full gate.

title: Scope CI to affected paths in a monorepo
description: Run only the checks relevant to what actually changed in a monorepo branch, so feedback time doesn't grow with the size of the whole repo.
why: Running the full suite on every change in a large monorepo means feedback time grows with the size of the whole repo, not the size of what actually changed.
scenario: A monorepo ran its entire test suite — including unrelated mobile and backend tests — on every single PR; a two-line frontend CSS fix took 40 minutes of CI before it could merge, until CI was scoped to only the paths actually changed.

title: Keep migrations coupled to the code that needs them
description: Ship a migration in the same branch/PR as the code depending on it, and make it backward-compatible to support a zero-downtime rolling deploy.
why: A migration merged separately from the code that depends on it can leave a window where the schema and the code expect different things, breaking a rolling deploy that mixes old and new instances.
scenario: A schema migration was merged separately from the feature code that depended on it, ahead of a rolling deploy; for several minutes, old app instances ran against the new schema and threw errors on every request until the code deploy caught up.

title: Don't merge past known-failing tests to unblock a deploy
description: Merging with red CI "just this once" erodes everyone's trust that a green `main` actually means something.
why: The first "just this once" sets a precedent — after enough exceptions, a green CI status stops meaning `main` is actually safe to deploy.
scenario: A team merged past a known-failing integration test "just this once" to hit a deadline; three more "just this once" merges later, a genuinely broken main went unnoticed for a day because nobody trusted the CI status enough to check it.

title: Encode the ticket ID in branch names
description: A convention like `feat/JIRA-123-add-export` makes any branch traceable back to the work item that justified it.
why: Without a traceable link back to the work item, understanding why a branch exists months later means reconstructing context from memory instead of just following the ID.
scenario: A branch named `fix/login-bug` with no ticket reference sat in the repo for a year; nobody could tell if it was safe to delete or represented an open issue, until the team required a ticket ID in every branch name going forward.

title: Audit stale branches periodically
description: Branches with no commits in months should be revived, merged, or deleted — not left indefinitely as clutter and confusion.
why: An abandoned branch nobody's touched in months is either forgotten work worth reviving or genuinely dead — left alone indefinitely, nobody can tell which.
scenario: A repo had over 80 branches with no commits in six months; a quarterly branch audit found most were safe to delete and a few represented genuinely abandoned work worth reviving, work that had been invisible clutter until then.

title: Scale branch protection to repository risk
description: A shared library used by many teams warrants stricter required checks than an internal tool only one team touches.
why: The review rigor a shared library needs to avoid breaking every downstream team is unnecessary overhead for a tool only one team uses — matching it to actual blast radius keeps both appropriately protected.
scenario: A shared internal library used by a dozen teams had the same lightweight review requirements as a single team's internal tool; after a breaking change in the library caused a multi-team outage, its branch protection was tightened to match its actual blast radius.

title: Avoid SELECT * in application code
description: Select only the columns you actually need — it reduces I/O, avoids breaking on schema changes, and lets covering indexes actually cover the query.
why: Pulling unused columns wastes I/O and network bandwidth, and a later schema change can break code that implicitly depended on column order or presence.
scenario: A dashboard query used `SELECT *` against a wide orders table; when a teammate added a large JSON audit column, dashboard load times doubled overnight because the query silently started pulling a column nobody needed.

title: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY
description: Add indexes for the columns that actually drive filtering, joining, and sorting on large tables, and confirm the benefit with an execution plan rather than assuming.
why: Without an index, the engine has to scan every row to find matches — on a large table that turns a millisecond lookup into a full-table scan.
scenario: A customer lookup by email took 4 seconds on a 20-million-row users table because no index existed on the email column; adding one dropped the same lookup to single-digit milliseconds.

title: Keep indexed columns sargable in WHERE clauses
description: Wrapping an indexed column in a function (`WHERE YEAR(CreatedAt) = 2024`) prevents an index seek — rewrite as a range comparison the optimizer can use.
why: Wrapping a column in a function forces the engine to evaluate that function against every row before it can compare, defeating the index's whole purpose of skipping rows.
scenario: A report filtered `WHERE YEAR(CreatedAt) = 2024` on a table with an index on CreatedAt; the function wrapper forced a full scan every night until it was rewritten as a range comparison the optimizer could actually seek on.

title: Always parameterize queries
description: String-concatenated SQL is both a SQL-injection vector and defeats the database's query plan cache — use parameters every time, no exceptions.
why: String-concatenated SQL lets user input change the meaning of the query itself — that's exactly what a SQL injection exploits, and parameters close that door structurally.
scenario: A search feature built its SQL by concatenating a search term directly into the query string; a penetration test showed an attacker could inject `' OR '1'='1` and dump the entire customer table, closed immediately by parameterizing the query.

title: Prefer set-based operations over row-by-row loops
description: A cursor or application-side loop processing one row at a time scales far worse than an equivalent set-based `UPDATE`/`INSERT` statement.
why: A row-by-row loop pays the overhead of a database round trip per row — a set-based statement does the same work in one round trip the engine can optimize as a whole.
scenario: A nightly job looped through 2 million rows one at a time issuing an UPDATE per row; rewriting it as a single set-based UPDATE statement cut the job from six hours to four minutes.

title: Keep transactions as short as possible
description: A long-running transaction holds its locks the whole time — minimize the work inside it to reduce blocking of other queries.
why: Every lock a transaction holds blocks other queries from touching the same rows — the longer the transaction runs, the longer everyone else waits.
scenario: A report-generation transaction stayed open for ninety seconds while formatting results outside the database; every other write to the same tables queued behind its locks, and moving the formatting outside the transaction fixed the blocking.

title: Use EXISTS instead of COUNT(*) > 0
description: `EXISTS` can stop scanning at the first match; `COUNT(*) > 0` typically has to count all matches first for no benefit when you only need a yes/no.
why: `COUNT(*)` has to tally every matching row before it returns, even though you only need to know if at least one exists — `EXISTS` can stop at the very first match.
scenario: A permissions check used `COUNT(*) > 0` against a table with millions of matching rows for a common role; switching to `EXISTS` let the engine stop at the first match instead of counting all of them, cutting the check's latency dramatically.

title: Avoid implicit type conversions in comparisons
description: Comparing a column to a literal of a different type (`WHERE VarcharCol = 123`) can silently disable index usage on that column.
why: Comparing a column to a mismatched-type literal forces the engine to convert every row's value to compare, which — just like wrapping the column in a function — silently disables the index.
scenario: A query compared an indexed VARCHAR order-number column to an integer literal; the implicit conversion silently disabled the index on every call, and the query ran as a full scan until the comparison type was fixed to match.

title: Use covering indexes for critical queries
description: A covering index lets the engine satisfy a frequently-run query entirely from the index, without a lookup back to the base table.
why: Without a covering index, the engine has to look up the index, then go back to the base table for the remaining columns — a second read for every row matched.
scenario: A frequently-run order-summary query needed three columns; adding a covering index let the engine answer it entirely from the index without a single lookup back to the base table, cutting its cost sharply.

title: Batch large bulk updates and deletes
description: Running one massive `UPDATE`/`DELETE` against millions of rows can blow out the transaction log and lock contention — batch it into smaller chunks.
why: A single massive UPDATE/DELETE holds its locks and grows the transaction log for the entire operation — batching keeps each unit of work, and its blocking window, small.
scenario: An engineer ran one `DELETE` against 50 million stale rows directly in production; it blew out the transaction log and blocked writes for twenty minutes until it was killed and rerun in smaller batches instead.

title: Keep statistics current
description: Stale statistics make the query optimizer misjudge row counts and pick bad plans as the underlying data grows — ensure auto-update is on or refresh manually after bulk loads.
why: The optimizer picks a plan based on its estimate of how many rows match — stale statistics from data that's grown since the last update lead it to a plan sized for data that no longer exists.
scenario: A table that grew from 10,000 to 10 million rows over a year kept using a query plan sized for the old row count because auto-update statistics had been disabled; a manual statistics refresh fixed a plan the optimizer had been silently getting wrong for months.

title: Use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN with a nullable subquery
description: `NOT IN` against a subquery that can return `NULL` silently returns zero rows for the whole query — `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have this trap.
why: If the subquery returns even one `NULL`, `NOT IN` can't determine the comparison is true or false for any row and silently returns nothing — a subtle correctness bug, not a performance one.
scenario: A "find users not in the excluded list" query used `NOT IN` against a subquery that could return NULL; a single NULL excluded-user row made the entire query silently return zero results, a correctness bug `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have.

title: Paginate at the query level
description: Use `OFFSET`/`FETCH` or keyset pagination in the query itself rather than loading a full result set and paging it in application code.
why: Loading a full result set and paging in application code means fetching and transferring every row just to discard most of them.
scenario: An API loaded an entire 500,000-row result set into memory and paged it in application code; switching to keyset pagination at the query level cut both memory usage and response time dramatically for the same endpoint.

title: Be explicit about join types
description: An accidental cross join or the wrong join type is one of the most common sources of duplicated or missing rows in a result set.
why: An unintended cross join or wrong join type doesn't usually error — it just silently returns the wrong number of rows, which is far harder to catch than a query that fails outright.
scenario: An implicit join between two tables in an older SQL dialect silently became a cross join after a WHERE clause was refactored; the report started returning duplicated rows for weeks before anyone noticed the row counts looked inflated.

title: Watch for N+1 queries from an ORM
description: A loop that triggers one query per iteration should be replaced with eager loading, an explicit join, or a projection that fetches everything in one round trip.
why: A loop issuing one query per iteration turns what should be a single round trip into hundreds or thousands, and latency compounds linearly with the size of the collection.
scenario: An ORM-backed order list page issued one query per order to fetch its line items in a loop; for a page showing 100 orders that meant 101 round trips, until eager loading collapsed it into two queries total.

title: Enforce integrity with constraints, not just app code
description: Foreign keys and `CHECK` constraints catch bad data regardless of which application or script wrote it — don't rely on application code alone.
why: A foreign key or check constraint is enforced by the database itself, so it catches bad data no matter which application or script wrote it — app-level validation only protects the one code path that runs it.
scenario: An application-only validation rule for unique emails had a bug that let a background import bypass it; two users ended up sharing an email until a database-level unique constraint caught what the application code had missed.

title: Rewrite correlated subqueries as joins where possible
description: A correlated subquery in the `SELECT` list re-executes per outer row on large result sets — an equivalent `JOIN` is usually far cheaper.
why: A correlated subquery re-executes once per outer row, so its cost scales with the outer result set size — a join usually lets the engine process the same logic as one set operation.
scenario: A report's SELECT list ran a correlated subquery per row to compute each customer's total spend; on 200,000 customers that subquery executed 200,000 times, until it was rewritten as a single join that computed it once per set.

title: Review indexes for unused or duplicate ones periodically
description: Every index adds write cost — an index that's never used by any query plan is pure overhead and should be dropped.
why: Every index has to be updated on every write, so an index no query plan actually uses is pure write overhead with zero corresponding read benefit.
scenario: A database audit found 40 indexes on a heavily-written table, a dozen of them never touched by any query plan in a year; dropping the unused ones measurably sped up writes with zero impact on any read.

title: Prefer UNION ALL unless you need de-duplication
description: Plain `UNION` forces an extra sort/distinct pass to remove duplicates — use `UNION ALL` when you know the sets don't overlap or duplicates are fine.
why: Plain `UNION` sorts and de-duplicates the combined result even when you already know there's no overlap, which is wasted work `UNION ALL` skips entirely.
scenario: A reporting query combined two non-overlapping result sets with plain `UNION`, forcing an unnecessary sort-and-dedupe pass on data that could never have duplicates; switching to `UNION ALL` removed that wasted work entirely.

title: Test query changes against realistic data volume
description: A plan that looks fine against a small dev database can degrade badly at production scale — test against a representative row count before shipping.
why: A query plan's cost is relative to table size — a plan the optimizer picks for a small dev table can become a very different, much worse plan once the table reaches production scale.
scenario: A query that ran fine against a 500-row dev database took 40 seconds in production against 50 million rows; the team started testing query changes against a production-scale snapshot after that surprise made it to a release.

title: Avoid leading-wildcard LIKE searches on large tables
description: `LIKE '%term'` can't use a standard b-tree index efficiently — consider full-text search or a trigram index for that access pattern instead.
why: A b-tree index is ordered by prefix, so a search with no fixed prefix can't use it to narrow the scan — the engine falls back to scanning every row.
scenario: A "search by partial name" feature used `LIKE '%smith%'` against a million-row customer table, forcing a full scan on every search; adding full-text search cut typical search latency from seconds to milliseconds.

title: Isolate analytical queries from transactional load
description: Route heavy reporting queries to a read replica or dedicated reporting store so they don't degrade OLTP performance for the primary workload.
why: A heavy reporting query competing for the same locks and I/O as transactional traffic can slow down or block the OLTP workload the business actually depends on in real time.
scenario: A finance team's month-end reporting queries ran directly against the production OLTP database and regularly slowed down checkout for real customers during that window, until reporting was routed to a read replica instead.

title: Verify execution plans before and after a change
description: Check the actual execution plan when adding an index or rewriting a query, not just whether the query returns the right rows.
why: A query can return the right rows while still using a much worse plan than intended — correctness and performance are separate questions, and only the plan answers the second one.
scenario: A new index was added to speed up a slow query, but nobody checked the execution plan afterward; the optimizer was still choosing the old table scan because a data-type mismatch silently prevented the new index from being used at all.

title: Make migrations additive first, cleanup later
description: Add new columns/tables in a backward-compatible way and defer destructive cleanup to a later migration, so old and new app versions can run side by side during a rolling deploy.
why: A destructive change like dropping a column the old app version still reads breaks whichever instances haven't been redeployed yet during a rolling deploy — additive-first keeps both versions working simultaneously.
scenario: A migration dropped a column the old app version still read during a rolling deploy; instances still running the old code started throwing errors on every request until the column was restored and the cleanup deferred to a later, additive-first migration.

title: Fix the join, don't paper over duplicates with DISTINCT
description: `SELECT DISTINCT` used to hide duplicate rows from a bad join usually means the join's cardinality is wrong — fix that instead of masking the symptom.
why: `DISTINCT` hides the symptom of a join with the wrong cardinality, but the underlying join is still processing and discarding duplicate rows — a mask that costs performance without fixing the bug.
scenario: A report wrapped its query in `SELECT DISTINCT` to hide duplicate rows coming from a fan-out join; the join was still processing and discarding the extra rows internally, and fixing the join's cardinality removed both the duplicates and the wasted work.

title: Choose appropriately sized data types
description: Storing dates as strings or defaulting every text column to `NVARCHAR(MAX)` costs both storage and index efficiency — pick types that match the actual data.
why: An oversized type like `NVARCHAR(MAX)` can't be indexed the same way a bounded type can, and it costs more storage and I/O per row than the data actually needs.
scenario: A table stored order dates as `NVARCHAR(MAX)` for flexibility; date-range queries couldn't use a normal index on it at all, and converting the column to a proper date type restored index usage and cut storage significantly.

title: Use window functions for running totals and ranking
description: `ROW_NUMBER()`, `SUM() OVER(...)`, and similar window functions usually outperform and outread an equivalent self-join or correlated subquery.
why: A self-join or correlated subquery computing a running total re-reads overlapping data for every row — a window function computes it in a single pass over the ordered set.
scenario: A running-balance report used a self-join to compute each day's cumulative total, re-scanning overlapping rows for every day; rewriting it with a `SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)` window function computed the same result in a single pass.

title: Monitor slow queries proactively
description: Review query store or slow-query logs on a schedule instead of only investigating performance after someone complains.
why: Waiting for a complaint means the slow query has already been degrading the experience for everyone hitting it, for however long it took someone to notice and report it.
scenario: A slow query degraded a checkout page for two weeks before a customer complaint finally surfaced it; after that the team started reviewing the slow-query log weekly instead of waiting to be told something was slow.

title: Avoid stacking views many levels deep
description: Deeply nested views make it hard for the optimizer to produce a good plan and hard for a human to debug what's actually being queried.
why: Each layer of nested views adds another level the optimizer has to unravel to build a plan, and a human debugging the final query has to trace through every layer to know what's actually being read.
scenario: A reporting view was built on top of four other nested views; when a number looked wrong, tracing what was actually being queried meant unraveling five layers by hand, and flattening it into one query made the logic auditable again.

title: Grant applications least-privilege database access
description: An application connecting as `sa`/`db_owner` by default has far more access than it needs — scope its credentials to the specific tables/operations it performs.
why: An application connecting as `db_owner` turns any injection or credential leak into full database compromise — scoped credentials limit what an attacker or a bug can actually do with that connection.
scenario: A web app connected to its database using the `sa` account for convenience; a routine SQL injection in an unrelated endpoint gave the attacker full database access instead of being contained to the handful of tables the app actually needed.

title: Apply least privilege by default
description: Grant only the permissions a user or service actually needs, and expand from there deliberately — never start broad and plan to narrow later.
why: Broad access granted "to be safe" or "for convenience" becomes the actual attack surface the moment that account or credential is compromised — narrowing it later rarely happens once things are working.
scenario: A reporting service was granted db_owner "to be safe" during a rushed launch; when a dependency vulnerability let an attacker run arbitrary queries through it months later, they had full database access instead of read-only access to two tables.

title: Assign permissions through roles, not per-user hacks
description: Use RBAC or ABAC so access can be reviewed and reasoned about, instead of scattering individual per-user permission checks through the codebase.
why: Per-user permission checks scattered through code can't be reviewed as a whole — nobody can answer "who can do X" without reading every code path, whereas a role can be audited in one place.
scenario: A codebase had `if (user.Id == 42 || user.Id == 87)` checks scattered through a dozen files granting special access to two specific people; when one left the company, nobody could confirm every place their access needed to be revoked, until it was replaced with a proper admin role.

title: Never commit secrets to source control
description: API keys, connection strings, and certificates belong in a secrets manager or vault with access auditing, never in a repository — even a private one.
why: Git history is effectively permanent — deleting a secret in a later commit doesn't remove it from history, and anyone with repo access can still recover it.
scenario: A contractor committed a production database password to a public GitHub repo; even after deleting it in the next commit, automated scanners had already found it in the git history within minutes, forcing an emergency credential rotation.

title: Prefer managed identity over static credentials
description: Use managed/workload identities for service-to-service auth in the cloud instead of long-lived static keys that have to be stored and rotated manually.
why: A static key sits waiting to be leaked or forgotten about until it expires — a managed identity has no long-lived secret to steal in the first place.
scenario: A legacy service stored a static Azure storage key in configuration that hadn't been rotated in three years; migrating to a managed identity removed the standing secret entirely, so there was nothing left for a leak to expose.

title: Require MFA for privileged accounts at minimum
description: Every administrative or highly privileged account should require MFA, with a roadmap toward requiring it for all users.
why: A password alone is one factor an attacker can obtain through phishing or reuse — MFA on the accounts with the most damage potential closes that gap where it matters most first.
scenario: An admin console had no MFA requirement; a phished password alone was enough for an attacker to log in as an administrator, an incident that led the company to mandate MFA on every privileged account within the week.

title: Rotate credentials on a schedule and on suspicion
description: Set a defined rotation cadence for keys and credentials, and rotate immediately on suspected compromise or when someone with access leaves.
why: A credential that never rotates is exactly as exposed today as it was the day it leaked, whether or not anyone knows it leaked — rotation puts a ceiling on how long a compromise stays useful.
scenario: A vendor integration's API key had been unchanged for five years and nobody remembered where it was even documented; when the vendor had a breach, the company couldn't quickly confirm whether that specific key had been exposed, because it had never been on a rotation schedule.

title: Prefer short-lived tokens over static ones
description: Use OAuth access tokens, SAS tokens, or similar short-lived credentials wherever the protocol supports them instead of a permanent static secret.
why: A stolen short-lived token expires on its own and limits an attacker's window — a stolen static secret stays valid until someone notices and manually revokes it.
scenario: A mobile app embedded a long-lived API key that a researcher extracted from the compiled binary; switching to short-lived OAuth tokens meant the same extraction only yielded a credential that expired within the hour.

title: Validate all external input at the trust boundary
description: Never trust client-supplied data — including hidden form fields and headers — validate and sanitize it where it enters the system.
why: Anything a client controls — including headers and hidden fields — can be forged; trusting it without validation lets an attacker send whatever the server will accept.
scenario: A checkout flow trusted a "price" value sent from a hidden form field instead of recalculating it server-side; a user modified the field in dev tools and successfully checked out a $500 item for one dollar.

title: Log authorization decisions for audit
description: Record who accessed what and whether it was allowed, not just application errors — it's what makes incident response and compliance audits possible.
why: Without a record of who accessed what and whether it was allowed, investigating a suspected breach means reconstructing events from incomplete or absent evidence.
scenario: During a suspected breach investigation, a security team discovered the application only logged errors, not authorization decisions; they couldn't determine who had accessed sensitive records or when, turning a contained incident into an open-ended, unresolved one.

title: Separate duties for sensitive operations
description: The person who can approve a production deploy shouldn't also be the only one who can alter the audit trail of that deploy.
why: If one person can both perform a sensitive action and alter its audit trail, that trail can't be trusted as independent evidence of what happened.
scenario: The same engineer who approved production deploys also had permission to edit the deployment audit log; after an unauthorized change was discovered, no one could prove the log itself hadn't been altered, undermining the entire investigation.

title: Use just-in-time access instead of standing admin rights
description: Grant elevated access only for the duration it's needed rather than leaving privileged roles active and unused most of the time.
why: Standing privileged access sits active and unused most of the time, which is exactly the window an attacker who compromises that account gets to work with — JIT shrinks that window to only when it's needed.
scenario: An engineer had standing admin rights to a production database used twice a year; when their laptop was compromised by malware, that always-on access became the attacker's path in, a window just-in-time access would have kept closed the other 363 days.

title: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit by default
description: Treat encryption as the baseline for all sensitive data, not an opt-in reserved for projects someone flagged as "sensitive".
why: Treating encryption as opt-in means it only gets applied to whatever someone remembered to flag as sensitive — data that wasn't flagged, but turns out to matter, ships unprotected.
scenario: A customer-support database table storing plaintext phone numbers was never flagged as "sensitive" by anyone, so it shipped unencrypted; a backup misconfiguration later exposed it directly, an incident encryption-by-default would have prevented regardless of whether anyone remembered to flag it.

title: Default to deny in access and network policies
description: Explicitly allow what's needed rather than trying to enumerate and block everything that's known-bad — default-allow policies age poorly.
why: A default-allow policy requires you to anticipate and block every bad case in advance — a default-deny policy only requires you to enumerate the good cases, a much smaller and more stable list.
scenario: A firewall configured to allow all outbound traffic except a manually maintained blocklist let a compromised server exfiltrate data to a new, unlisted destination; switching to default-deny with an explicit allowlist would have blocked the unlisted destination automatically.

title: Scope IAM policies to specific resources
description: Avoid wildcard resource grants (`*`) even for development convenience — scope policies to the specific resource IDs/ARNs a role actually needs.
why: A wildcard resource grant means a compromised credential for one task can reach every resource that policy covers, not just the one it was actually meant for.
scenario: A CI pipeline's IAM role was granted `s3:*` on `*` "for convenience" during setup; when a dependency vulnerability compromised the pipeline, the attacker could read and modify every S3 bucket in the account instead of just the one build-artifacts bucket the pipeline actually needed.

title: Review access on a regular cadence
description: Audit unused accounts, stale service principals, and orphaned permissions periodically, not only when a compliance audit forces the question.
why: Access naturally accumulates as people change roles or leave, and without a periodic review it just keeps growing — nobody's job is to notice unless it's someone's job to look.
scenario: A quarterly access review, done for the first time in two years, found 40 former employees' accounts still active and a service principal from a project cancelled three years earlier still holding write access to production.

title: Manage access at the group/role level
description: Assigning permissions to groups instead of individuals keeps access reviewable and consistent as people move between teams.
why: Individual permission assignments have to be manually updated every time someone changes teams — group-based access updates automatically just by changing group membership.
scenario: A company managed file-share access per individual user for years; when a reorg moved 30 people between teams in one week, IT couldn't keep up with the individual permission changes, and several people retained access to their old team's sensitive files for months.

title: Add conditional access for sensitive systems
description: Require signals like device compliance or sign-in risk in addition to a password for access to sensitive systems, not a password check alone.
why: A stolen password alone is often enough to authenticate — requiring an additional signal like device compliance means a stolen credential isn't sufficient on its own to get in.
scenario: A stolen password alone was enough to log into a finance system from an unmanaged personal device in another country; adding conditional access requiring a compliant, enrolled device blocked that exact login pattern from working again.

title: Centralize identity through an IdP
description: Use SSO via an identity provider (Entra ID, Okta) instead of maintaining separate local credential stores per application.
why: Separate local credential stores per application mean a person's access has to be individually revoked in every single one when they leave — centralized identity revokes everywhere at once.
scenario: Twenty internal tools each had their own local username/password store; when an employee was terminated, IT had to manually track down and disable access in all twenty, and missed two of them for a month, until SSO through a single IdP centralized revocation.

title: Enforce authorization at every reachable layer
description: Apply the same auth checks at the API, admin panel, and background job trigger level — don't rely on the UI being the only gate to a sensitive action.
why: If the UI is the only place authorization is checked, anyone who calls the API or triggers the job directly — bypassing the UI entirely — bypasses the check too.
scenario: A delete-user feature was only guarded by hiding the button in the UI for non-admins; a support agent who called the backend API directly with the right ID was able to delete accounts anyway, because the API itself never checked the caller's role.

title: Classify data and match controls to sensitivity
description: Apply stronger controls to more sensitive data rather than treating all data uniformly — classification should drive the control, not the other way around.
why: Applying the same controls to all data uniformly means either over-protecting low-value data at real cost, or under-protecting the sensitive data that actually needs it.
scenario: A company applied the same encryption and access controls to marketing copy and to customer social security numbers alike; the actual sensitive data ended up under-protected relative to its risk once the team started classifying data and matching controls to sensitivity.

title: Design every grant to be quickly revocable
description: A token, role assignment, or shared credential should be revocable on its own, without requiring a system-wide credential rotation to shut off access.
why: A shared credential that can only be shut off by rotating it everywhere means revoking access for one person disrupts access for everyone else who shares it.
scenario: A shared API key used by three different internal integrations had to be rotated for all three at once when one team's usage looked suspicious, breaking the other two teams' working integrations in the process — a cost that per-integration scoped tokens would have avoided.

title: Treat anything shipped to a client as public
description: Never embed secrets in client-side code, mobile apps, or CI logs — anything that reaches a client or a log should be assumed to be exposed.
why: Client-side code, mobile binaries, and CI logs can all be extracted or read by anyone with access to them — a secret embedded there is functionally already leaked.
scenario: A mobile developer hardcoded a backend API key directly into the app for convenience; within a day of release, the key had been extracted from the app binary and was being used by unrelated third parties to call the API for free.

title: Use one service account per application
description: A dedicated service principal per application scopes blast radius and keeps auditing meaningful, versus one shared account used by several systems.
why: A shared service account makes it impossible to tell which application actually performed a given action from the audit log, and a leak in one app compromises every app sharing that credential.
scenario: Three internal tools shared one service account against the database; when suspicious activity showed up in the audit log, the team couldn't tell which of the three tools had actually performed the queries, and had to investigate all three instead of one.

title: Rate-limit and lock out authentication attempts
description: Backoff and lockout on repeated failed logins slow down credential-stuffing and brute-force attacks against your authentication endpoints.
why: Without a slowdown on repeated failures, an attacker can try credentials as fast as the network allows — brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks depend entirely on that speed.
scenario: A login endpoint with no lockout let an attacker attempt 50,000 password guesses per minute against a list of leaked credentials; adding backoff and lockout after a handful of failed attempts made the same attack impractically slow.

title: Patch known vulnerabilities on a schedule
description: Most real-world breaches exploit known, unpatched CVEs rather than novel zero-days — keep dependencies and base images current on a defined cadence.
why: Most real breaches exploit a vulnerability that already had a patch available — the gap between patch release and patch application is the actual window attackers use.
scenario: A breach was traced back to a web server dependency with a CVE that had been patched by the vendor eight months earlier; the company just hadn't applied it, exactly the pattern behind most real-world breaches — a known, unpatched hole rather than a novel exploit.

title: Review IAM policy changes like code
description: Permission grants are high-impact — require peer review and change management for IAM policy edits themselves, not just application code.
why: A permission grant is high-impact and easy to get wrong in a way that's hard to notice — an over-broad policy looks the same as a correct one until it's actually exploited.
scenario: An engineer widened an IAM policy from one specific S3 bucket to a wildcard `*` to unblock themselves quickly, with no review; the overly broad grant sat unnoticed for a year until a routine audit caught it, exactly the kind of change peer review for IAM edits is meant to catch immediately.

title: Isolate environments with separate credentials
description: Dev, test, and prod should use separate access boundaries so a compromised dev credential can't reach production.
why: Shared credentials between dev and prod mean a comparatively weakly-protected dev environment becomes a path into production for anyone who compromises it.
scenario: A developer's dev-environment credentials, reused for convenience in a staging config that also had a path to prod resources, were phished; because dev and prod shared no credential boundary, the compromise reached production data it was never supposed to be able to touch.

title: Prefer delegated OAuth scopes over sharing one powerful credential
description: Federated, scoped authorization limits what a compromised integration can do, versus one broad credential shared across multiple integrations.
why: One broad credential shared across integrations means compromising the weakest integration compromises everything that credential can reach — scoped, delegated tokens limit each integration's blast radius.
scenario: A single powerful API key was shared across five third-party integrations; when one integration partner had a breach, the company had to assume all five were compromised and rotate everything, instead of revoking just the one delegated, scoped token that partner actually held.

title: Plan incident response assuming leaks happen
description: Have a tested process to revoke and rotate credentials quickly — prevention matters, but assume it will eventually fail and plan the response too.
why: Prevention eventually fails somewhere — without a tested response process, discovering a leak in the moment means improvising credential rotation and revocation under pressure instead of following a known plan.
scenario: A company discovered a leaked API key during a routine audit but had no defined process for what to do next; rotating it, confirming what it had accessed, and notifying affected teams took three improvised days instead of the few hours a rehearsed incident response plan would have taken.

title: Test your break-glass procedure
description: Document and periodically test the emergency access path that must work even when your normal IdP/SSO is unavailable.
why: An emergency access path that's never been tested is exactly as likely to work as any other undocumented, unexercised process — precisely the time you can't afford it to fail is during the emergency it's meant for.
scenario: When the company's SSO provider had an outage, nobody could log in to anything, including the emergency break-glass account, because its credentials had been rotated into the same SSO-managed vault a year earlier and never actually tested since.

title: Be specific and concrete in prompts
description: Vague prompts force the model to guess your intent — state the desired format, constraints, and success criteria explicitly instead of assuming it infers them.
why: An ambiguous request has many valid-looking answers, and the model has no way to know which one you actually meant — specificity narrows the space to the answer you want.
scenario: A developer asked an assistant to "clean up this function" with no further detail; it reformatted the style but left the actual bug untouched, because the request never stated that fixing the null-check bug was the actual goal.

title: Give the model relevant context, not everything
description: Include the specific facts, code, or constraints the task needs — not your entire history or every file in the repo "just in case".
why: Irrelevant context doesn't just cost tokens, it dilutes the signal — the model has to work harder to figure out what's actually relevant, which increases the odds it focuses on the wrong thing.
scenario: An engineer pasted an entire 4,000-line service file into a prompt just to ask about one 10-line helper function; the assistant's answer ended up mixing in unrelated context from the rest of the file instead of focusing on the one function that mattered.

title: Show the model an example of the output you want
description: One concrete example of the desired format or style (few-shot) often steers output more reliably than a paragraph of abstract instructions.
why: A model imitating a concrete example has less room to misinterpret your description of "concise" or "formal" than one trying to infer those qualities from adjectives alone.
scenario: A team kept getting API response formats that were technically correct but not what they wanted; pasting one concrete example JSON response into the prompt got a matching format on the very next try, no further description needed.

title: State constraints explicitly, don't assume defaults
description: Say what should NOT change, which files are off-limits, or what approach to avoid — the model can't infer a boundary you never mentioned.
why: The model optimizes for a plausible answer to the literal prompt — anything you leave unsaid is fair game, so an unstated constraint gets violated as often as it gets guessed correctly.
scenario: An assistant asked to "refactor the auth module" quietly renamed a public method other services depended on; the next prompt explicitly said "don't rename any public method signatures," and the resulting refactor left the public surface untouched.

title: Break large tasks into smaller steps
description: Ask for one well-defined step at a time, or use a planning step first, rather than one giant prompt covering an entire multi-part task.
why: A model reasoning over a large, multi-part task in one pass is more likely to drop a requirement — smaller steps are individually easier to get right and to verify.
scenario: A request to "migrate our whole API to a new framework" in one shot produced a plausible-looking but subtly broken result missing several endpoints; breaking it into one endpoint-group at a time let each step be verified before moving to the next.

title: Iterate instead of writing the perfect prompt upfront
description: Treat the first response as a draft — refine with follow-up corrections rather than trying to anticipate every requirement in one exhaustive initial prompt.
why: It's often faster to correct a close answer than to predict every edge case in advance, and the model's own draft frequently reveals ambiguities you hadn't thought to specify.
scenario: An engineer spent twenty minutes writing an exhaustive upfront prompt trying to anticipate every edge case for a data-migration script; a colleague got a working draft in two exchanges by accepting a rough first pass and correcting the two edge cases it actually missed.

title: Tell the model what "done" looks like
description: Define acceptance criteria — tests passing, a specific output format, a behavior to verify — instead of leaving success open to interpretation.
why: Without a concrete definition of done, neither you nor the model has an objective way to tell whether the output actually satisfies the request or just looks plausible.
scenario: A request to "add tests for this module" produced tests that passed but didn't actually assert anything meaningful; specifying "tests must fail if the discount calculation is off by even one cent" as the acceptance criteria produced tests that genuinely caught the next regression.

title: Separate instructions from the data they operate on
description: Clearly delineate the actual task instructions from any pasted content (code, logs, documents) the model should read or transform.
why: A model can't reliably tell where your instruction ends and pasted content begins unless you mark the boundary — that ambiguity is also how prompt injection from untrusted content sneaks in.
scenario: A prompt pasted a customer's raw support message directly after the instructions with no delimiter; the message happened to contain the phrase "ignore previous instructions," and the assistant's response changed behavior accordingly until the data was clearly fenced off from the instructions.

title: Ask the model to explain its reasoning for non-trivial decisions
description: For a design choice or debugging conclusion, ask for the reasoning behind it, not just the final answer.
why: A plausible-sounding answer with no visible reasoning is harder to verify — seeing the reasoning lets you catch a flawed assumption before you act on a wrong conclusion.
scenario: An assistant recommended switching a service to eventual consistency; asking it to explain the reasoning surfaced that it had assumed a traffic pattern the actual service didn't have, letting the engineer catch the flawed assumption before implementing the wrong architecture.

title: Correct mistakes directly instead of restarting the conversation
description: Point out specifically what was wrong and why, in the same conversation, rather than abandoning it and starting a fresh prompt from scratch.
why: A fresh prompt throws away the context the model already built up about your actual intent — a direct correction lets it fix just the wrong part while keeping everything it got right.
scenario: An engineer's first prompt produced code that was almost right except for one wrong SQL join; instead of starting over, they said "the join in step 3 is wrong, it should be a LEFT JOIN on order_id" and got the fix in one turn instead of regenerating everything.

title: Use system/role instructions for standing preferences
description: Put durable preferences — coding style, tone, constraints that apply to every request — in a persistent instruction file instead of repeating them each time.
why: Repeating the same preferences in every prompt wastes tokens and is easy to forget — a standing instruction applies automatically without you having to remember to restate it.
scenario: A team kept re-explaining their code style and testing conventions in every single prompt for weeks; moving those standing preferences into a persistent instructions file meant every new session followed them automatically without anyone retyping them.

title: Match your prompt's detail to the task's ambiguity
description: A well-defined, narrow task needs less scaffolding than an open-ended or judgment-heavy one — don't over-specify the trivial and under-specify the ambiguous.
why: Over-specifying a simple task wastes effort on ceremony that doesn't change the outcome, while under-specifying a genuinely ambiguous one leaves the actual risk unaddressed.
scenario: A one-line "rename this variable" request got padded with paragraphs of unnecessary context and constraints out of habit; meanwhile a genuinely ambiguous "design our new permissions model" request got a two-sentence prompt that left the actual hard tradeoffs unaddressed.

title: Trim conversation history instead of letting it grow unbounded
description: Summarize or clear stale context — resolved subtasks, superseded file contents — instead of carrying a long session's full history forward indefinitely.
why: Every prior message the model re-reads costs tokens on every subsequent turn, and irrelevant history dilutes the model's attention on what's actually still relevant.
scenario: A long debugging session accumulated hours of exploratory dead-end context; every subsequent response got slower and less focused until the stale exploration was summarized down to its conclusion and the irrelevant history dropped.

title: Reference files instead of pasting their full contents
description: When the model can read a file itself through a tool, point it at the file path rather than pasting the entire contents into the prompt.
why: Pasted content is duplicated into every subsequent turn of the conversation, while a file reference the model reads on demand is paid for once, not repeatedly.
scenario: A developer pasted the full contents of a 2,000-line config file into a prompt so the assistant could look up one setting; pointing it at the file path instead let it read exactly what it needed without bloating every following turn with the full file's text.

title: Ask for a diff or targeted change, not a full file rewrite
description: When editing existing code, ask for the specific change rather than having the model reproduce the entire file in its response.
why: Reproducing an unchanged 500-line file to alter three lines spends nearly all its output tokens restating what already exists — the useful signal is a tiny fraction of the response.
scenario: A request to fix one broken import caused the assistant to reproduce an entire 800-line file with the one-line fix buried somewhere inside it; asking for a targeted diff instead made the actual change immediately visible and easy to verify.

title: Cache and reuse stable context across requests
description: Where the platform supports prompt caching, structure prompts so stable content — system instructions, unchanging reference material — comes first and stays identical across calls.
why: A cache hit on unchanged content skips reprocessing it entirely — a prompt where the same prefix repeats verbatim turns repeated full-price reads into cheap cache hits.
scenario: A team restructured their prompts so a long, unchanging set of system instructions came first and only the task-specific part varied per call; the unchanged prefix started hitting the prompt cache, cutting both latency and cost on every subsequent request.

title: Scope tool output to what's actually needed
description: Request a specific line range, a filtered search, or a summary instead of dumping an entire large file or unfiltered command output into context.
why: An unfiltered search result or a whole large file consumes context budget with mostly-irrelevant content, crowding out room for the parts that actually matter to the task.
scenario: An agent investigating a slow endpoint dumped an entire 50,000-line log file into context looking for one error; filtering to just the error-level lines from the relevant time window found the same root cause in a fraction of the tokens.

title: Avoid asking the model to repeat information it already produced
description: Refer back to an earlier answer — "use the function you just wrote" — instead of asking the model to restate it in full before continuing.
why: Regenerating already-produced content is pure overhead — it adds no new information and just spends tokens reproducing what's already sitting in the conversation.
scenario: A prompt asked the assistant to "write out the full function again" just to reference it in a follow-up question; referring back to "the function you wrote above" got the same answer without regenerating hundreds of already-correct tokens.

title: Choose the smallest capable model for routine subtasks
description: Route simple, well-defined subtasks — formatting, extraction, classification — to a smaller/cheaper model and reserve a larger one for genuinely hard reasoning.
why: A task a small model handles reliably doesn't get better results from a larger one — it just costs more per token for the same outcome.
scenario: A team routed every task, including simple date-format conversions, to their most expensive model by default; switching routine formatting and extraction subtasks to a smaller model cut costs sharply with no drop in quality on those specific tasks.

title: Close out finished subtasks instead of keeping them live
description: Once a subtask is verified complete, let it drop out of active context — via summarization or a new session — rather than keeping its full exploration history live.
why: Exploration that led to a dead end or a now-resolved question still costs tokens on every future turn if it stays in context, even though its useful conclusion could be captured in one line.
scenario: A long multi-part project kept every resolved subtask's full exploration live in context for the whole session; summarizing each finished subtask down to its one-line conclusion once verified kept later turns faster without losing anything that actually mattered.

title: Verify AI output before relying on it
description: Treat a model's answer as a draft to check, especially for facts, citations, or security-sensitive code — not as ground truth by default.
why: A model can produce a fluent, confident-sounding answer that's factually wrong with no visible signal distinguishing it from a correct one — verification is the only reliable defense.
scenario: An assistant cited a specific legal statute number in a compliance draft that turned out not to exist; the team that had a policy of verifying every AI-cited reference caught it before it went to a client, and the one that didn't have that policy nearly shipped it as fact.

title: Keep a human in the loop for high-stakes or irreversible actions
description: Require explicit review and approval before an AI-driven action that's destructive, hard to reverse, or affects shared systems — deployments, deletions, financial transactions.
why: An AI agent can act confidently on a flawed premise just as easily as a correct one, and for irreversible actions there's no way to undo the consequence of it being wrong.
scenario: An autonomous coding agent was given permission to run `git push --force` without confirmation; it force-pushed over a colleague's unmerged commits while "cleaning up" a branch, an outcome a human-in-the-loop check before any irreversible git operation would have caught.

title: Give the model tools instead of asking it to simulate them
description: Where accuracy matters — a calculation, a live lookup, running actual code — connect the model to a real tool rather than relying on it to produce the answer from memory or estimation.
why: A model asked to compute or recall something a tool could do exactly is prone to a plausible-looking but wrong answer — a real tool call replaces that guess with an actual, checkable result.
scenario: An assistant asked to calculate a complex compound-interest figure from memory got the formula subtly wrong; the same request routed through an actual calculator tool call returned the exact, checkable number instead of a plausible-looking approximation.

title: Don't treat model confidence as a proxy for correctness
description: A firmly-stated answer isn't more likely to be right than a hedged one — the model's tone doesn't track its actual certainty the way a human expert's does.
why: Models are trained to produce fluent, assertive text regardless of whether the underlying claim is well-supported, so confident phrasing carries much less evidential weight than it does from a person.
scenario: A junior engineer accepted a confidently-worded architecture recommendation without question, because it "sounded sure of itself"; the recommendation turned out to rest on an incorrect assumption about the team's traffic pattern that a more skeptical read would have caught.

title: Match the task to what the model is actually good at
description: Lean on AI for drafting, summarizing, exploring options, and pattern-matching across large context — and lean less on it for tasks needing guaranteed precision or novel judgment with no precedent.
why: A model's strength is statistical pattern completion over what it's seen before — tasks that fit that shape go well, and tasks requiring guaranteed exactness or genuinely novel judgment are where it's most likely to confidently miss.
scenario: A team asked an assistant to make a final, unreviewable call on a novel multi-million-dollar vendor contract negotiation strategy; it performed far better a week later drafting and summarizing the same team's meeting notes, a task that actually fit its strength in pattern completion over precedent-setting judgment.

title: Review AI-generated code as carefully as human-written code
description: Apply the same review standards — security, edge cases, test coverage — to AI-authored changes as to a human contributor's PR, not a lighter pass because it "looks clean".
why: AI-generated code can look idiomatic and well-formatted while still containing a logic error or security gap — fluency in style is not the same signal as correctness.
scenario: An AI-generated PR looked clean and idiomatic, so a reviewer approved it with a lighter pass than usual; it shipped a SQL injection vulnerability that a normal-depth review, applied regardless of who or what authored the code, would have caught.

title: Be explicit about what the AI should NOT do
description: For an agent with access to real systems, state boundaries — files it shouldn't touch, actions that need confirmation — rather than assuming it will infer them from good judgment alone.
why: A model without an explicit boundary acts on the literal scope of the request, which can be broader than what you actually intended it to touch.
scenario: An agent given broad filesystem access to "clean up the repo" deleted an entire directory of generated fixtures a test suite actually depended on; explicitly scoping what it shouldn't touch beforehand would have prevented the outage that followed.

title: Build feedback into your AI workflow, not just the final output
description: Correct the model's intermediate assumptions or plan before it executes on them, rather than only reviewing the finished result.
why: Catching a wrong assumption at the planning stage costs one correction — catching the same wrong assumption after a full implementation is built on top of it costs redoing the implementation too.
scenario: An agent was given a large multi-file refactor task and only reviewed at the very end; the plan it had silently formed in the first step rested on a wrong assumption about the module boundaries, and the whole implementation had to be redone once that surfaced — a check at the planning stage would have cost one correction instead of a full redo.

title: Understand the limits of the model's knowledge cutoff
description: For anything that depends on recent events, current versions, or live data, have the model verify against a live source rather than relying on training data with a cutoff date.
why: A model answering from memory about anything after its training cutoff is extrapolating, not recalling — it can produce a fluent answer about a library version or event it was never actually trained on.
scenario: A team asked an assistant which cloud SDK version was current and got a confident answer naming a version that had since been deprecated; having it check the actual package registry instead of relying on training-data memory caught the mismatch before it shipped.

title: Treat AI as a collaborator to direct, not an oracle to defer to
description: Bring your own judgment to an AI's suggestion — push back, ask for alternatives, and make the final call yourself rather than accepting the first answer because it sounds authoritative.
why: The model doesn't have your full context, stakes, or accountability for the outcome — deferring to it as an oracle transfers a decision to something with less information about the situation than you have.
scenario: An engineer accepted an assistant's first proposed database schema without pushback, since it "sounded right"; a colleague who instead pushed back and asked for two alternative designs ended up catching a normalization issue that would have been expensive to fix after data started flowing in.

title: Build one immutable artifact and promote it through every environment
description: Build the container image (or package) exactly once per commit, tag it with the commit SHA, and deploy that same artifact to staging and then production — never rebuild from source for each environment.
why: Rebuilding per environment means what passed testing in staging isn't provably what's running in prod — a different dependency resolution, base image patch, or build-time environment variable could produce a subtly different artifact. Promoting the identical, already-scanned and already-tested image removes that gap entirely.
scenario: A deployment pipeline rebuilt the Docker image separately for staging and production; a base-image security patch landed between the two builds, and the version that passed staging tests wasn't the exact bits that shipped to prod, until the team switched to building once and promoting the same tagged image.

title: Make automated checks a hard gate, not an advisory one
description: Configure the pipeline so a failing test, security scan, or lint step stops the deployment outright, with no manual override path in the normal flow — not a status that's merely displayed for a human to weigh.
why: A gate anyone can click past under deadline pressure isn't a gate, it's a suggestion — and the one time it gets overridden to hit a date is usually the time it mattered. Removing the override path is what actually lets deployment be automatic without a human needing to compensate for the gate's weakness.
scenario: A failing security scan had a "proceed anyway" button that got clicked under deadline pressure to hit a launch date; the exact vulnerability it flagged was exploited in production three weeks later, and the override path was removed from the pipeline after that.

title: Roll production changes out progressively, never all at once
description: Use a canary or blue-green strategy that exposes a new deployment to a small slice of production traffic first, and only widen to 100% after that slice looks healthy.
why: A bug that reaches 100% of traffic instantly turns a deploy into an outage; the same bug caught at 5% of traffic is a contained incident affecting a fraction of users for a much shorter window, and gives automation time to catch it before it spreads further.
scenario: A bad deploy pushed to 100% of traffic instantly took checkout down for every user simultaneously; the same bug caught at a 5% canary stage the next release only affected a small slice of users before automated rollback caught it.

title: Trigger rollback from metrics automatically, don't wait for a human to notice
description: Wire the deployment pipeline to watch error rate, latency, and saturation during a rollout and automatically revert to the previous artifact the moment a defined threshold is breached.
why: The gap between "a bad deploy going out" and "someone noticing the dashboard" is where most of the damage from a bad deploy actually happens. A metrics-triggered auto-rollback closes that gap to roughly the length of one monitoring interval instead of however long it takes a human to be looking at the right graph.
scenario: A memory leak in a new deploy went unnoticed for 40 minutes until an on-call engineer happened to check a dashboard; after wiring automatic rollback to error-rate thresholds, an equivalent regression the following month reverted itself within two minutes of the metric crossing the line.

title: Scan the built artifact for vulnerabilities before it is allowed to deploy
description: Run a dependency and container-image vulnerability scan (e.g. Trivy, Snyk) against the exact artifact that will ship, as a blocking pipeline stage, in addition to scanning source code with SAST.
why: A source-code scan alone misses vulnerabilities introduced by the base image or a transitive dependency pulled in only at build time — scanning the final artifact catches the actual thing about to run in production, not just the code that produced it.
scenario: A source-code security scan came back clean, but the base container image it was built on had a known critical CVE that only a scan of the final built artifact caught before it ever reached production.

title: Run automated smoke tests immediately after every deployment
description: After a new version reaches an environment (staging or a production canary), automatically hit its critical paths (login, checkout, the top few endpoints) and fail the pipeline if they don't respond correctly, before traffic is widened further.
why: Pre-deploy tests run against a build; smoke tests run against the actual deployed instance with its real configuration, network policies, and secrets wired up — catching an entire class of "worked in CI, broken in the real environment" failures that no amount of pre-deploy testing can see.
scenario: A build passed every unit and integration test in CI, then failed immediately in production because a required environment variable was misconfigured only in that environment; an automated post-deploy smoke test hitting the login endpoint would have caught it before traffic was widened.

title: Separate "deployed" from "released" using feature flags for risky changes
description: Ship a risky change to production behind a feature flag that defaults off, and enable it for real users as a separate, instantly reversible step from the deployment itself.
why: Continuous deployment means code reaches prod constantly, which is only safe if reaching prod doesn't automatically mean reaching every user — a flag lets you turn a risky feature off in seconds without a rollback (a new deployment) at all, and lets you separate 'is the code broken' from 'is the feature a bad idea' as two independently reversible decisions.
scenario: A risky new checkout flow was deployed straight to 100% of users with no flag; when it broke, the only way to stop the bleeding was a full rollback (a new deployment). The next risky change shipped behind a feature flag instead, so disabling it took one config toggle and seconds, not a redeploy.

title: Rent buffers from ArrayPool<T> for short-lived, large arrays
description: In hot paths that repeatedly allocate large temporary arrays (parsing, buffering, serialization), rent from `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` and return it instead of letting each call allocate and discard a new array.
why: A large short-lived array allocated on every call becomes GC pressure the moment call volume climbs — a pooled buffer reuses the same memory instead of asking the GC to reclaim it over and over.
scenario: A file-processing service allocated a fresh 1MB byte array for every uploaded document; under concurrent uploads the GC became the bottleneck until the buffers were rented from ArrayPool<T> and returned after each parse.

title: Pass large readonly structs with in
description: For a struct bigger than a few fields that a hot-path method only reads, pass it with `in` rather than by value to avoid copying it on every call.
why: Passing a large struct by value copies every field on every call — `in` passes a reference instead, and the cost of the copy disappears entirely from a path that runs thousands of times a second.
scenario: A pricing engine passed a 200-byte pricing-context struct by value into a method called millions of times per batch run; switching the parameter to `in` removed the copy overhead and measurably shortened the nightly batch window.

title: Drop LINQ for plain loops once profiling shows it matters
