description: LINQ reads well and is fine by default, but a profiler-confirmed hot loop with iterator and delegate overhead is a legitimate place to fall back to a plain `for`/`foreach`.
why: Every LINQ operator in a chain is its own iterator with delegate invocation overhead — in a loop that runs millions of times, that overhead is measurable, but rewriting code that isn't actually hot just trades readability for nothing.
scenario: A real-time bidding service's hot LINQ chain over millions of bids per second showed up clearly in a profiler as iterator overhead; rewriting just that one loop as a plain for-loop was the single change that got the service under its latency budget.

title: Use TryGetValue instead of ContainsKey plus an indexer lookup
description: `if (dict.TryGetValue(key, out var value))` does one lookup; `if (dict.ContainsKey(key)) { var value = dict[key]; }` does two for the same result.
why: ContainsKey followed by the indexer hashes and walks the bucket twice for a value you already found the first time — TryGetValue gets the same answer in a single lookup.
scenario: A cache-lookup hot path called `ContainsKey` followed by an indexer read on every request, hashing the same key twice; switching to `TryGetValue` halved the lookup cost on a service handling tens of thousands of requests per second.

title: Use source-generated regex for patterns used repeatedly
description: Mark a frequently-used pattern with `[GeneratedRegex(...)]` (or cache a compiled `Regex` instance) instead of constructing `new Regex(pattern)` on every call.
why: Constructing a `Regex` parses and (if compiled) JIT-compiles the pattern every single time — a source-generated or cached instance pays that cost once instead of on every invocation.
scenario: A log-parsing service constructed a new `Regex` object for every single line it processed; switching to a source-generated regex cut CPU usage sharply once the pattern was compiled once instead of re-parsed millions of times a day.

title: Stream large sequences with IAsyncEnumerable<T> instead of materializing them
description: When a caller only needs to iterate a large result once, yield it as `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` rather than building the full `List<T>` in memory before returning it.
why: Materializing the full sequence forces the whole result set into memory at once even though the caller only ever looks at one item at a time — streaming keeps memory use proportional to one item, not the whole set.
scenario: An export endpoint built a `List<Order>` of two million rows in memory before streaming it to the client, causing memory spikes that occasionally triggered OOM kills; switching to `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` kept memory flat regardless of export size.

title: Pool expensive-to-construct objects on hot paths
description: Use `ObjectPool<T>` for objects that are costly to allocate and reset cheaply (buffers, parsers, formatter instances) rather than constructing and discarding a fresh one per call.
why: An object that's expensive to construct but trivial to reset is exactly the case pooling is built for — reconstructing it every call pays the expensive part repeatedly for no benefit.
scenario: An image-processing pipeline constructed a fresh, expensive-to-initialize encoder object per image; pooling and reusing encoder instances cut per-image latency and reduced GC churn during bulk thumbnail generation.

title: Pick the collection type for the access pattern, not out of habit
description: Use `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` for key lookups, `HashSet<T>` for membership checks, and `List<T>` for ordered iteration — not `List<T>.Contains()` for something that's really a membership test.
why: `List<T>.Contains` is an O(n) scan; the equivalent `HashSet<T>.Contains` is O(1) — the wrong default collection turns a cheap check into a linear scan that gets slower as the data grows.
scenario: A permissions check used `allowedUserIds.Contains(userId)` against a `List<int>` that grew to tens of thousands of entries, turning a supposedly fast check into a visible slowdown; switching the collection to a `HashSet<int>` made the check effectively instant regardless of size.

title: Skip ToList()/ToArray() calls that only feed a single enumeration
description: Materializing a LINQ query mid-pipeline only pays off if you iterate the result more than once — a single `foreach` afterward can consume the `IEnumerable<T>` directly.
why: A `ToList()` that's only enumerated once allocates a full copy of the sequence for no reuse benefit — the lazy `IEnumerable<T>` would have produced the same single pass without the extra allocation.
scenario: A report generator called `.ToList()` on a LINQ query it only ever enumerated once in a single foreach loop afterward; removing the unnecessary materialization cut one avoidable full-collection allocation from every report run.

title: Use StringComparison.Ordinal for non-linguistic comparisons
description: Comparing identifiers, keys, or file paths should use `StringComparison.Ordinal`/`OrdinalIgnoreCase` explicitly — the culture-aware default is both slower and semantically wrong for non-linguistic text.
why: Culture-aware comparison applies locale-specific linguistic rules to text that was never meant to be compared linguistically, which is both extra CPU work and a source of subtle bugs when the deployment culture differs from the dev machine's.
scenario: A username-lookup comparison used the culture-aware default string comparison, and the exact same username failed to match itself once the server's OS locale was changed during a migration; switching to `StringComparison.Ordinal` fixed both the bug and a measurable CPU cost.

title: Measure elapsed time with Stopwatch, not DateTime subtraction
description: Use `Stopwatch`/`Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()` for measuring durations in code — `DateTime.Now`/`UtcNow` has coarser resolution and can jump if the system clock is adjusted mid-measurement.
why: A system clock adjustment (NTP sync, manual change) between two `DateTime.Now` reads can make an elapsed-time calculation go negative or wildly wrong — `Stopwatch` is backed by a monotonic counter that a clock change can't disturb.
scenario: A performance test's timing measurements briefly showed negative durations after an NTP clock sync adjusted the system clock mid-run; switching from `DateTime.Now` subtraction to `Stopwatch` eliminated the impossible negative numbers for good.

title: Cache reflection-derived metadata instead of re-reflecting per call
description: Look up `PropertyInfo`/`MethodInfo` or compile an expression-based accessor once and cache it (a static `ConcurrentDictionary` keyed by type) rather than reflecting fresh on every invocation.
why: Reflection lookups are meaningfully slower than a direct member access, and the metadata for a given type never changes at runtime — reflecting again on every call pays that cost for an answer that was already known.
scenario: A serialization library re-reflected the same type's properties on every single call; caching the compiled accessor in a static dictionary after the first lookup cut serialization time dramatically for a service processing high call volume.

title: Set initial collection capacity when the size is already known
description: Pass a capacity hint to `new List<T>(count)`/`new Dictionary<K,V>(count)` when you already know roughly how many items will go in, instead of letting the collection resize itself repeatedly.
why: Growing a `List<T>` without a capacity hint means it reallocates and copies its backing array each time it fills up — a known size up front avoids every one of those intermediate reallocations.
scenario: A nightly import built a `List<T>` of two million records with no capacity hint, forcing dozens of silent reallocations and copies as it grew; setting the initial capacity to the known row count removed that overhead entirely.

title: Cache CultureInfo and format providers used inside loops
description: Resolve `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` or a `NumberFormatInfo` once outside a loop instead of re-resolving it on every formatting call inside the loop body.
why: Re-resolving the same culture/format provider on every iteration repeats work whose result never changes within the loop — hoisting it out is a one-line change that removes that repeated cost entirely.
scenario: A report-formatting loop re-resolved `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` on every one of a million formatting calls; hoisting it once outside the loop was a one-line change that measurably sped up the report.

title: Batch related calls to a dependency instead of looping single round-trips
description: When a loop calls the same downstream API/database once per item, look for a batch/bulk overload that does it in one round-trip instead of N.
why: Each round-trip pays a fixed latency cost regardless of how little data it carries — a hundred single-item calls pay that fixed cost a hundred times where one batched call pays it once.
scenario: A sync job called a partner's API once per record across 50,000 records every night, each call paying the same 100ms round-trip latency; switching to the partner's batch endpoint cut the job from over an hour to a few minutes.

title: Project EF Core queries into DTOs instead of loading full entities
description: Use `.Select(x => new SomeDto { ... })` to pull only the columns an endpoint actually needs, rather than materializing the full entity graph and discarding most of it.
why: Loading every column and navigation property to use three fields sends far more data over the wire and through change tracking than the endpoint actually needs.
scenario: An orders list endpoint materialized the full `Order` entity graph, including unused navigation properties, just to return three fields to the UI; projecting directly into a DTO cut both the query time and the payload size significantly.

title: Use AsNoTracking() for read-only EF Core queries
description: Any query whose results won't be modified and saved back should call `.AsNoTracking()` to skip EF Core's change-tracking bookkeeping entirely.
why: Change tracking snapshots every tracked entity so EF Core can detect modifications later — for a query that never modifies anything, that bookkeeping is pure overhead with no payoff.
scenario: A read-only reporting endpoint used a normal EF Core query, paying full change-tracking overhead for data that was never going to be saved back; adding `.AsNoTracking()` measurably reduced its memory footprint and latency.

title: Compile hot, frequently-repeated EF Core queries
description: Use `EF.CompileAsyncQuery` for a query shape that runs constantly with only parameter values changing, so LINQ-to-SQL translation happens once instead of on every call.
why: EF Core re-translates the LINQ expression into SQL on every call unless the query is compiled — for a query executed thousands of times a minute, that repeated translation is pure waste.
scenario: A pricing lookup query ran the same shape thousands of times a minute, re-translating identical LINQ into SQL every single call; compiling it once with `EF.CompileAsyncQuery` removed that repeated translation cost from the hot path.

title: Split multi-collection Include chains instead of letting them cross-join
description: Loading two or more collection navigations in one query via `Include().ThenInclude()` produces a cartesian product in the generated SQL — split into separate queries (or use `AsSplitQuery()`) when that matters.
why: A single query joining two one-to-many collections returns rows multiplied across both collections, so the result set EF has to deserialize and de-duplicate can be far larger than the actual data returned.
scenario: An order-detail query used `Include().ThenInclude()` to pull both line items and comments in one query, and the cross-joined result set for a large order came back with tens of thousands of duplicated rows; splitting it into two queries fixed both correctness and performance.

title: Enable response compression only for compressible, non-sensitive payloads
description: Turn on Brotli/Gzip response compression for large, text-based, cacheable responses — not blindly for every endpoint, especially ones with sensitive content.
why: Compressing an already-small or already-compressed payload (like a small JSON error body or an image) burns CPU for no bandwidth benefit, and compressing responses that vary per secret can leak information through timing/size side channels.
scenario: A team enabled response compression globally, including on a personalized endpoint whose payload size varied based on secret account details; a researcher demonstrated a timing/size side-channel that leaked account information, and compression was scoped back to safe, cacheable responses only.

title: Share cross-cutting logic through endpoint filters, not per-endpoint copies
description: Minimal API endpoint filters or route groups let validation, logging, or auth checks apply once to a group of routes instead of being pasted into every handler.
why: Logic copied into every handler has to be updated in every handler when it changes — a shared filter applied to the group means one edit covers all of them.
scenario: Six different minimal API handlers each duplicated the same authentication and logging logic pasted into every one; a change to the auth check had to be manually applied six times and was missed in one, until the logic moved into a shared endpoint filter applied once to the whole route group.

title: Tune Kestrel and thread-pool settings from load-test data
description: Set `MinThreads`, connection limits, and request queue length based on what an actual load test shows the service needs — not the framework defaults or a guess.
why: The default thread-pool ramp-up is tuned for a generic workload, not yours — under a sudden burst, an under-tuned minimum thread count causes exactly the latency spike load testing exists to catch before production does.
scenario: A service running with default Kestrel thread-pool settings showed a sharp latency spike at the start of every traffic burst; a load test revealed the minimum thread count was under-provisioned for the real burst pattern, and tuning it from load-test data smoothed out the spike.

title: Cache expensive computed values with an explicit TTL
description: A value that's expensive to compute and requested repeatedly with the same inputs belongs in `IMemoryCache`/a distributed cache with a TTL you chose deliberately, not an accidental TTL from copying another cache entry's settings.
why: Recomputing an expensive value on every request wastes CPU on work whose answer hasn't changed, but a copied TTL that doesn't match this value's actual staleness tolerance either serves stale data too long or recomputes needlessly often.
scenario: A dashboard aggregation query took two seconds and was requested constantly with the same inputs; caching it with a TTL chosen deliberately for how stale the business could tolerate the numbers being cut load on the database sharply without serving noticeably outdated data.

title: Return the lightest result type that fits
description: Use `Results.NoContent()`/`NoContent()` instead of serializing an empty object, and `Results.Empty` over a placeholder DTO, when there's genuinely nothing to return.
why: Serializing an empty or placeholder object still runs the full JSON serialization pipeline for a response that carries no actual information.
scenario: A delete endpoint serialized an empty placeholder object on every successful call; switching to `NoContent()` removed a full JSON-serialization pass for a response that never carried any actual information.

title: Await the async EF Core call, not its synchronous counterpart
description: Use `ToListAsync()`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync()`, and `SaveChangesAsync()` inside an async pipeline — calling the synchronous version blocks a request thread on I/O it should have awaited.
why: A synchronous EF Core call inside an otherwise-async request handler blocks the thread for the duration of the database round-trip, which is exactly the cost async was introduced to avoid.
scenario: A request handler called `.ToList()` (the synchronous EF Core method) instead of `.ToListAsync()` inside an otherwise fully async pipeline; under load that one blocking call was enough to starve the thread pool until it was corrected.

title: Paginate any endpoint that could return an unbounded result set
description: Add skip/take or keyset pagination to a list endpoint before the underlying table grows large enough to make an unpaginated call slow or memory-heavy.
why: An endpoint that returns 'all rows' works fine while the table is small and quietly becomes a multi-second, memory-heavy response the moment the table grows — pagination caps the cost regardless of table size.
scenario: An "all customers" endpoint worked fine at launch with 500 rows and quietly became a 4-second, multi-megabyte response once the table passed a million rows; adding pagination capped the cost regardless of how large the table grew.

title: Warm up the app before it takes production traffic
description: Exercise critical code paths right after startup (a warm-up request, ReadyToRun/AOT compilation) so the first real users don't pay the JIT tiering cost a fresh instance incurs.
why: A freshly started instance runs its first requests through slower, not-yet-optimized JIT tiers — without a warm-up, that latency lands on whichever real user happens to hit the instance first after a deploy.
scenario: The first user to hit a freshly deployed instance consistently saw a multi-second delay while the JIT warmed up; adding a startup warm-up request against the critical checkout path moved that cost off real users and onto the deploy process itself.

title: Use bulk-write APIs for large batched inserts
description: For inserting or updating large numbers of rows, use `SqlBulkCopy`/an EF Core bulk-extensions package instead of calling `SaveChanges()` once per row.
why: Calling `SaveChanges()` per row means a separate round-trip and transaction overhead for every single row — a bulk API does the same work in a fraction of the round-trips.
scenario: A data migration called `SaveChanges()` once per row across 3 million records, taking most of a day; switching to `SqlBulkCopy` for the bulk insert cut the same migration down to under twenty minutes.

title: Match DI service lifetime to actual state, not habit
description: A stateless service with no per-request data has no reason to be registered as scoped or transient — registering it as a singleton avoids allocating a new instance every time.
why: A scoped registration for a service that holds no per-request state allocates a fresh instance on every request for no reason — the lifetime should reflect whether the service actually needs isolation, not just copy whatever the last registration used.
scenario: A completely stateless currency-formatting service was registered as Scoped out of habit, allocating a new instance on every single request for no reason; re-registering it as a Singleton removed that pointless per-request allocation.

title: Resolve a scoped service once per request, not repeatedly
description: Inject a scoped dependency once via the constructor and reuse the reference, rather than resolving it from `IServiceProvider` again each time it's needed within the same request.
why: Re-resolving the same scoped instance repeatedly adds container lookup overhead for a reference the constructor already handed you once — there's no second instance to gain from resolving it again.
scenario: A request handler resolved the same scoped `IUserContext` from `IServiceProvider` five separate times across different methods within one request; injecting it once via the constructor and reusing the reference removed four redundant container lookups per request.

title: Put enough context in exception messages to diagnose from the trace alone
description: Include the operation being attempted and the relevant input values (never secrets) in an exception message, so a stack trace on its own points at the cause instead of just the symptom.
why: "Object reference not set to an instance of an object" tells you nothing about which object or why — a message naming the operation and input turns a guessing exercise into a direct fix.
scenario: An on-call engineer got paged with only "Object reference not set to an instance of an object" in the stack trace and spent an hour reproducing the bug locally to find the cause; the fix included the failing order ID and operation name in the exception message so the next occurrence was diagnosable from the alert alone.

title: Use distinct custom exception types per failure category
description: Define specific exception types (`OrderNotFoundException`, `PaymentDeclinedException`) instead of throwing a generic `Exception` for every failure — it lets callers and logs distinguish cause without parsing a message string.
why: A generic `Exception` gives a caller nothing to catch selectively or a log nothing to group by — a distinct type turns "something failed" into "this specific, known failure happened", which is what both code and dashboards need to react correctly.
scenario: A payment service threw a generic `Exception` for every failure mode, so a caller couldn't distinguish "card declined" from "network timeout" without parsing the message text; splitting them into distinct exception types let the UI show the right message and the dashboard group failures by real cause.

title: Wrap third-party exceptions at the boundary, preserving the original
description: Catch an SDK/library-specific exception at the integration boundary and rethrow your own exception type with the original set as `InnerException`, so callers depend on your contract, not the vendor's.
why: Callers that catch a vendor-specific exception type couple your whole codebase to that vendor's error hierarchy — wrapping it gives you a stable contract while `InnerException` keeps the original diagnostic detail one click away.
scenario: A codebase caught and directly rethrew a third-party SDK's `SdkTimeoutException` all over the codebase; when the vendor changed their SDK's exception hierarchy in a major version bump, every one of those catch blocks broke, instead of the one wrapping layer that would have needed updating if the boundary had been properly wrapped.

title: Ask an AI reviewer to specifically hunt for swallowed exceptions
description: Beyond a general review pass, prompt an AI code review for empty catch blocks, catches that only log at Debug level, and catches missing a rethrow — a targeted pass a human skim often misses.
why: A swallowed exception produces no crash and no obvious symptom, so it's exactly the kind of defect a normal review skim glides past — pointing an AI review at that specific pattern catches what a general-purpose read is prone to miss.
scenario: A routine review missed an empty `catch (Exception) { }` block silently swallowing a failed inventory update for weeks; a follow-up review specifically prompted to hunt for swallowed exceptions caught the same pattern in a different service before it caused the same silent data gap.

title: Log the full exception object, not just ex.Message
description: Pass the exception instance to the logger (`_logger.LogError(ex, "...")`) so the stack trace, inner exceptions, and any custom data travel with the log entry instead of being discarded.
why: `ex.Message` alone throws away the stack trace and inner exception chain — exactly the information that tells you where the failure actually originated instead of just where it was caught.
scenario: An incident investigation had only `ex.Message` in the logs, which said "Value cannot be null" with no stack trace to say where; after switching to logging the full exception object, the next similar failure pointed straight at the exact line and inner exception that caused it.

title: Retry each independent operation on its own, not the whole workflow
description: Wrap each retryable step (one API call, one DB write) with its own backoff policy (Polly) instead of retrying an entire multi-step workflow when only one step actually failed.
why: Retrying the whole workflow re-runs steps that already succeeded, which is wasted work at best and a duplicated side effect at worst — retrying just the failed step limits the retry to where it's actually needed.
scenario: A checkout workflow retried its entire five-step process whenever step four (email confirmation) failed, silently re-charging the customer's card as part of the retry; giving each step its own independent retry policy stopped the payment step from ever being retried unnecessarily.

title: Emit business-level metrics, not just technical ones
description: Track counters for things the business cares about (orders placed, payments failed, signups completed) alongside request/latency metrics, so a functional regression shows up on a dashboard.
why: A service can look perfectly healthy on CPU, memory, and latency while a bug silently drops every third order — only a business-level metric would show that regression before a customer complaint does.
scenario: A checkout service looked perfectly healthy on every technical dashboard — CPU, latency, error rate — while a bug silently dropped every third order; a business-level "orders placed" metric would have shown that drop the moment it started instead of waiting for a customer complaint.

title: Add a circuit breaker around unreliable dependencies
description: Wrap calls to a flaky downstream dependency in a circuit breaker (Polly) that fails fast once it's clearly down, instead of letting every caller queue up on a timeout.
why: Without a breaker, every caller independently waits out the full timeout against a dependency that's already known to be down, which multiplies one outage into thread-pool exhaustion across every caller.
scenario: A downstream recommendation service went down, and every request to the main app started queuing up waiting for it to time out, exhausting the thread pool and taking the whole app down with it; a circuit breaker that failed fast once the dependency was known-down would have contained the blast radius to just recommendations.

title: Turn unexpected internal state into a loud, logged failure
description: When code hits a state that should be impossible (a switch's supposedly-exhaustive default case, a null that invariants say can't happen), throw and log loudly instead of quietly falling back to a default value.
why: A silent fallback for "impossible" state hides the fact that an assumption was actually violated — the bug still happened, it just now surfaces as a different, harder-to-trace symptom somewhere downstream instead of at its actual source.
scenario: A supposedly-exhaustive switch's default case silently returned a fallback value instead of throwing; a new enum value added months later hit that silent fallback and produced wrong behavior for weeks before anyone traced it back to the swallowed "impossible" case.

title: Emit distributed tracing spans, not just a correlation-ID field
description: Use `ActivitySource`/OpenTelemetry to create spans around significant operations, so a trace viewer can show the actual timing breakdown across a request — not just a shared ID to grep logs by.
why: A shared correlation ID lets you find every log line for a request, but a span tree tells you which specific step in that request actually took the time — the second question is usually the one that matters during troubleshooting.
scenario: A slow checkout request had a correlation ID that let an engineer find every log line for it, but not which specific step actually took the eight seconds; adding distributed tracing spans around each step pointed straight at a slow third-party fraud-check call the log lines alone never could have isolated.

title: Give every external dependency its own named health check
description: Register a separate `IHealthCheck` per dependency (database, cache, each downstream API) rather than one aggregate check, so a failing dependency is named, not just "unhealthy".
why: An aggregate health check that just says "unhealthy" still leaves you guessing which dependency is actually down — a named check per dependency turns the health endpoint itself into the first step of triage.
scenario: A single aggregate `/health` endpoint just said "unhealthy" during an incident, and the on-call engineer had to manually check the database, cache, and three downstream APIs one by one to find which was actually down; splitting it into named per-dependency checks turned that into a one-glance answer.

title: Have AI explain the failure mode a change introduces, not just that it compiles
description: When reviewing an AI-suggested change, explicitly ask it to describe how the new code could fail — what input, timing, or dependency state would break it — rather than accepting "this should work".
why: A model confirming its own code compiles and looks reasonable isn't the same signal as it having reasoned about failure modes — asking directly for the failure mode surfaces the edge case before it ships instead of during an incident.
scenario: An AI-suggested caching change looked clean and compiled fine; asked directly how it could fail, the same assistant identified that concurrent writes during a cache refresh would return stale data to some callers, an edge case that a plain "does it compile" check never surfaced.

title: Use idempotency keys for externally-triggered operations
description: For a webhook receiver, message handler, or payment endpoint that might be retried or redelivered, dedupe on an idempotency key stored per request rather than trusting the caller to send it exactly once.
why: A network blip or an at-least-once delivery guarantee means the same request will eventually arrive twice — without a stored idempotency key, the second delivery re-executes a side effect that was only supposed to happen once.
scenario: A payment provider's webhook was redelivered after a network blip, and the handler processed it a second time, double-charging a customer; adding an idempotency key check made the redelivered webhook a safe no-op instead of a duplicate charge.

title: Record before/after state for auditable, state-changing operations
description: For operations where being able to answer "what changed and from what" matters (account changes, permission grants, financial adjustments), log or store the prior and new value, not just that a change happened.
why: A log line that only says "value updated" gives an investigator nothing to work with — capturing what it changed from and to is what actually lets a 2am incident be reconstructed instead of guessed at.
scenario: A support team investigating a customer's complaint that their subscription tier changed unexpectedly found only a log line saying "plan updated" with no record of the before or after value; after the team started logging prior and new state on such changes, the next similar ticket was resolved in minutes instead of being unanswerable.

title: Return a typed Result with a reason code at service boundaries
description: Have a service method return a `Result<T>`/error-object with a specific, enumerable reason code instead of a bare `bool`/`null` or a string message that has to be parsed to know what actually went wrong.
why: A bare `false` or `null` tells the caller something failed but not what or why, forcing them to re-derive the reason — a typed reason code is both machine-checkable by the caller and a direct, searchable signal when it shows up in a log.
scenario: A service method returned a bare `false` on failure with no explanation; callers across the codebase had no way to tell "user not found" from "insufficient balance" from "service unavailable" without re-deriving it, until it was replaced with a typed Result carrying a specific reason code each caller could branch on.

title: Check in reviewed, idempotent migration SQL instead of trusting runtime auto-migration
description: Generate the migration's SQL script and review/commit it, and apply it through a controlled deploy step — don't call `Database.Migrate()` blindly on every instance's startup.
why: A migration nobody reviewed can silently do something destructive that only shows up once it's already run against production — a checked-in, reviewed script catches that before it executes, and running it once as a deploy step avoids every instance racing to apply it simultaneously.
scenario: An instance configured to call `Database.Migrate()` on every startup scaled out to five replicas during a deploy, and all five raced to apply the same migration simultaneously, corrupting the schema; switching to a single reviewed migration step in the pipeline removed the race entirely.

title: Expose the running build's version on a /version endpoint
description: Return the commit SHA, build number, and deploy timestamp from a simple `/version` (or `/health`) endpoint, so after any deploy or rollback you can confirm what's actually running without guessing from a dashboard.
why: "Did the rollback actually take effect?" is unanswerable from application behavior alone when a bug is subtle — a version endpoint gives a direct, unambiguous answer in one request instead of an inference from symptoms.
scenario: After a rollback during an incident, the on-call engineer couldn't tell from application behavior alone whether the rollback had actually taken effect yet; hitting the `/version` endpoint gave an immediate, unambiguous answer instead of guessing from symptoms.

title: Keep the previous artifact ready so rollback is a redeploy, not a rebuild
description: Retain the last several tagged container images/packages in the registry so reverting means pointing the deployment at an already-built, already-tested artifact — not rebuilding from an old commit under pressure.
why: Rebuilding from an old commit during an incident risks a different result than what actually ran before (a dependency that's since moved, a different base image patch level) — redeploying the exact prior artifact has none of that uncertainty.
scenario: During an incident, an engineer tried to "rebuild from the last known-good commit" under pressure, and the rebuild pulled a since-updated transitive dependency that behaved subtly differently than what had actually been running in production; redeploying the exact previously-built artifact instead would have avoided that uncertainty entirely.

title: Fail fast and loudly at boot on invalid configuration
description: Validate required configuration (connection strings, secrets, feature-critical settings) during startup and throw immediately with a clear message if something's missing, rather than starting successfully and failing mysteriously on the first request that needs it.
why: An instance that starts "successfully" with broken config looks healthy to the orchestrator right up until real traffic hits the code path that needed the missing setting — failing at boot turns a confusing runtime mystery into an obvious, immediate deploy failure.
scenario: A service started up "successfully" with a missing database connection string and looked healthy to the orchestrator for twenty minutes until the first real request needed it and failed with a confusing null-reference exception; validating config at boot would have failed the deploy immediately with a clear message instead.

title: Make readiness checks verify real dependency reachability
description: A readiness probe should actually attempt to reach the database/cache/downstream API it depends on (with a tight timeout), not just return 200 because the process is running.
why: A readiness check that only confirms the process is alive will happily pass traffic to an instance that can't actually reach its database — the check exists specifically to catch that gap, and a check that always passes doesn't.
scenario: A readiness probe just returned 200 as long as the process was alive; an instance that had completely lost its connection to the database still received live traffic and failed every single request, until the probe was changed to actually attempt a database ping.

title: Run database migrations as one explicit deploy step
description: Apply schema migrations from a single controlled step in the pipeline, not from application startup code that every scaled-out instance would otherwise try to run at once.
why: Several instances racing to apply the same migration on startup can deadlock each other or apply it more than once — a single explicit step removes that race entirely.
scenario: Ten scaled-out instances each tried to run the same schema migration from their own startup code during a rolling deploy, and two of them deadlocked against each other mid-migration; moving the migration to one explicit pipeline step removed the race for good.

title: Log a structured startup banner on every boot
description: Emit one structured log line at startup containing the version, environment, and effective config source(s), so "which build is this and what does it think its environment is" is answerable from logs alone.
why: Reconstructing which build and config an instance booted with, after the fact, from scattered evidence is far slower than reading the one log line that stated it outright the moment the process started.
scenario: An on-call engineer investigating a bug couldn't tell which config source (environment variable vs. appsettings vs. key vault) an instance had actually loaded at boot; after adding a structured startup banner logging that explicitly, the next investigation answered the same question in seconds by reading one log line.

title: Test the rollback path itself in staging
description: Actually exercise reverting to the previous version in staging as part of your deploy process, not only the forward deploy — an untested rollback script is as likely to fail as any other unexercised procedure.
why: The one time you need rollback to work is during an incident, under pressure — that's the worst possible moment to discover the rollback script itself has a bug nobody caught because nobody ever ran it.
scenario: A team assumed their rollback script worked because it had never been run; during a real incident it turned out the script referenced an environment variable that had been renamed months earlier, and the rollback itself failed, doubling the outage — a staging rehearsal would have caught it in advance.

title: Validate options classes at startup, not mid-request
description: Register `IValidateOptions<T>` (or data annotations) on bound configuration classes so a missing or malformed setting fails app startup instead of surfacing as a confusing null-reference deep in a request handler.
why: A bad config value that isn't validated at startup surfaces instead as whatever downstream error it happens to cause — often a null-reference or cast exception far from the actual cause — where startup validation would have named the real problem immediately.
scenario: A malformed connection-string setting wasn't validated at startup and surfaced three hours later as a confusing cast exception deep inside a request handler nobody connected back to the config; registering `IValidateOptions<T>` would have failed the same bad config at boot with a message naming the actual problem.

title: Keep production diagnostic tooling enabled
description: Enable `dotnet-trace`, `dotnet-dump`, and `dotnet-counters` (or their container-friendly equivalents) against production instances so a live issue can be captured in the moment, without restarting or redeploying the process to add instrumentation.
why: An issue that only reproduces under real production load is usually gone by the time you redeploy with extra logging to catch it — live diagnostic tooling captures the actual failing process state instead of waiting for a reproduction that may never come back.
scenario: A memory-usage spike only reproduced under real production traffic and was gone by the time a redeploy with extra logging went out to try to catch it; live `dotnet-trace` capture against the actual running instance caught the exact allocation pattern causing it without ever needing a redeploy.

title: Tag global unhandled-exception logs with request path and trace ID
description: The global exception handler's log entry should include the request path, method, and trace/correlation ID, so an alert on it points straight at the failing endpoint instead of requiring a log search to find it.
why: An alert that just says "unhandled exception occurred" sends the on-call engineer straight into a log search to even find which endpoint broke — including the path and trace ID in the alert itself skips that first, avoidable step.
scenario: An unhandled-exception alert just said "unhandled exception occurred" with no further detail, sending the on-call engineer straight into a log search across a dozen endpoints to even find which one broke; tagging the alert with the request path and trace ID skipped that entire search step.

title: Use AI to flag error-rate and log-pattern shifts right after a rollout
description: Have an AI-assisted step compare error logs and rates from just after a deploy against the pre-deploy baseline, surfacing new exception types or spikes early enough to decide on a rollback before a human would have noticed manually.
why: The gap between a bad deploy going out and a human noticing the dashboard is where most of the damage happens — an automated comparison against baseline catches a new failure pattern in the first few minutes instead of the first few hours.
scenario: A bad deploy quietly introduced a new exception type at a low but steady rate that nobody noticed on the aggregate error-rate dashboard for two days; an automated post-deploy comparison against the pre-deploy baseline would have flagged the new exception pattern within minutes of the rollout.

title: Smoke-test the rollback artifact, not just the forward one
description: Confirm the "known good" previous build still boots and passes basic smoke tests against current infrastructure and config before treating it as a safe rollback target.
why: Infrastructure and config keep moving forward even when the application version doesn't — a previous build that was fine months ago can silently no longer be compatible with today's environment, and the only way to know is to have actually tested it recently.
scenario: A team treated last month's build as a safe rollback target without re-testing it, and during a real incident the "known good" build turned out to be incompatible with a config change made since then, so the rollback itself failed; smoke-testing the rollback artifact regularly would have caught the incompatibility before it was needed for real.

title: Keep the Data Protection key ring compatible across versions you might roll back to
description: Confirm that a rollback target can still decrypt cookies/tokens issued under the current version's key ring and payload shape, before relying on rollback as a fast recovery path for an auth-adjacent bug.
why: If the rolled-back version can't read tokens the newer version issued, the 'fast recovery' rollback actually logs out every active user — a rollback plan that doesn't account for this finds out the hard way, mid-incident.
scenario: A team rolled back to fix an unrelated bug during an incident, and the older version couldn't decrypt the auth cookies the newer version had issued, logging out every active user as a side effect of the "fast recovery"; checking Data Protection compatibility ahead of time would have surfaced that risk before it happened mid-incident.

title: Fix bad settings with a config push before reaching for a rollback
description: Use `IOptionsMonitor<T>`-backed reloadable configuration for anything likely to need a fast correction, so a bad setting is fixed by pushing new config, not by redeploying or rolling back the whole application.
why: A bad config value doesn't need the code reverted, it needs the value changed — treating every fix as a rollback means waiting for a full deploy cycle to fix something a live config reload could have corrected in seconds.
scenario: A bad feature-flag percentage caused a spike in errors, and the team's first instinct was to roll back the entire deployment, a ten-minute process; because the flag was backed by `IOptionsMonitor`-driven reloadable config, they instead pushed a corrected config value that took effect in seconds with no redeploy at all.
